about: Worked-example calculators (docs/anp-spec.md section 8.6). Each calculator is data: inputs, derived values as expressions, worked steps as templates, reference ranges, what the answer means, and a practice generator. {key} in a template prints that value; {key:2} forces 2 decimals; {key:+} adds a sign. Scored item id: calculators:<id>:practice. Validator: scripts/lib/anp-tool-checks/calculators.mjs.

calculators.title: Flow, pressure gradient and resistance
calculators.intro: A pressure gradient pushes fluid and resistance holds it back. Enter the pressure at each end of a tube and the tube's resistance to find the flow.
calculators.formula: F = ΔP ÷ R

invalid.text: Make the inlet pressure higher than the outlet pressure. With no pressure difference there is no gradient to push fluid from inlet to outlet, and if the outlet were higher, fluid would flow the other way.
Resistance must be greater than zero.

steps.title: Find the pressure gradient
steps.text: ΔP = P1 − P2 = {P1} mm Hg − {P2} mm Hg = {dP} mm Hg. Only the difference between the two ends matters, not how high the pressures are.

steps.title: Write the flow equation
steps.text: F = ΔP ÷ R: flow rises with the gradient and falls with resistance.

steps.title: Substitute, keeping the units
steps.text: F = {dP} mm Hg ÷ {R} mm Hg per mL/min

steps.title: Calculate and cancel the units
steps.text: {dP} ÷ {R} = {F}. The mm Hg on the top and bottom cancel, leaving mL/min. F = {F} mL/min.

results.label: Flow
results.normal: There is no single normal value for a tube: flow is whatever ΔP and R allow.

meaning.text: A gradient of {dP} mm Hg pushes {F} mL/min through this resistance. Double the gradient and flow doubles to {F2} mL/min; double the resistance and flow halves to {Fhalf} mL/min. Raise both pressures by the same amount and nothing changes, because the gradient is the same.

asks.prompt: Fluid flows through a tube. The pressure at the inlet is {P1} mm Hg and the pressure at the outlet is {P2} mm Hg. The tube's resistance is {R} mm Hg per mL/min. What is the flow?

A pump holds the start of a rubber tube at {P1} mm Hg, and the far end drains into a container at {P2} mm Hg. The tube has a resistance of {R} mm Hg per mL/min. How much fluid flows through it each minute?

calculators.title: Radius and resistance: the fourth-power rule
calculators.intro: Resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius<sup>4</sup> (Poiseuille). Change a tube's radius while the pressure gradient stays the same, and see what happens to resistance and flow.
calculators.formula: R ∝ 1 ÷ r<sup>4</sup>, so at the same ΔP, new F = old F × (r<sub>new</sub> ÷ r<sub>old</sub>)<sup>4</sup>

inputs.label: New radius as a fraction of the old one
inputs.hint: 0.5 means half the radius; 2 means double.

invalid.text: The radius fraction must be greater than zero.
Enter a flow greater than zero.

steps.title: Write the rule
steps.text: Resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius<sup>4</sup>. Length and viscosity have not changed, so only the radius term matters, and ΔP stays the same.

steps.title: Raise the radius change to the fourth power
steps.text: ({f})4 = {f} × {f} × {f} × {f} = {f4}. The new radius4 is {f4} times the old one.

steps.title: Find the change in resistance
steps.text: Resistance changes by 1 ÷ {f4} = {Rx}, so the new resistance is {Rx} times the old resistance.

steps.title: Find the new flow
steps.text: At the same ΔP, flow changes by the inverse of the resistance change: F = {F0} mL/min × {f4} = {F1} mL/min.

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: {F1} ÷ {F0} = {Fx}, so the new flow is {pct}% of the original, from a radius that is {pctR}% of the original.

meaning.text: Narrowing the radius to {pctR}% cut flow to {pct}%. The drop is far bigger than the change in radius, because radius counts four times over. To push the original {F0} mL/min through the narrowed tube, the pressure gradient would have to rise {Rx}-fold. That is why a small change in the radius of a tube is a far stronger control of flow than a change in pressure.

Widening the radius to {pctR}% raised flow to {pct}% of the original: a {pctR}% radius gives a {Fx}-fold flow, because radius counts four times over. A small widening is a powerful way to increase flow without raising the pressure gradient.
With the radius unchanged, resistance and flow are unchanged.

asks.prompt: A tube carries {F0} mL/min. Its radius changes to {f} times its original value ({pctR}% of the original radius), while the pressure gradient, length and viscosity stay the same. What is the new flow?

calculators.title: Stroke volume and ejection fraction
calculators.intro: Stroke volume is how much blood one ventricle ejects in one beat. Ejection fraction is what share of its filled volume that is. Enter the ventricle's volume at the end of diastole and at the end of systole.
calculators.formula: SV = EDV − ESV;  EF = SV ÷ EDV × 100%

inputs.label: End-diastolic volume
inputs.hint: Typical at rest: about 120 mL (roughly 100 to 160).

inputs.label: End-systolic volume
inputs.hint: Typical at rest: about 50 mL (roughly 35 to 70).

invalid.text: End-systolic volume must be smaller than end-diastolic volume. The ventricle ejects blood during systole, so it holds less at the end of systole than at the end of diastole.

steps.title: Stroke volume is what the ventricle ejects
steps.text: SV = EDV − ESV = {EDV} mL − {ESV} mL = {SV} mL per beat.

steps.title: Ejection fraction is the share of the filled volume ejected
steps.text: EF = SV ÷ EDV = {SV} mL ÷ {EDV} mL = {EFf}. The mL cancel, so EF has no units.

steps.title: Convert to a percentage
steps.text: {EFf} × 100 = {EF}%. The other {left}% of the blood (the ESV) stays in the ventricle.

results.label: Stroke volume
results.normal: About 60 to 100 mL per beat in a resting adult.

results.label: Ejection fraction
results.normal: About 50 to 70 percent. 40 percent or less is called reduced.

meaning.text: An EF of {EF}% means the ventricle ejects less than two-fifths of the blood it holds. A value of 40% or less is the cutoff clinicians use for a ventricle that contracts weakly. The blood left behind raises the ESV, so the next beat starts from a fuller ventricle.
An EF of {EF}% is below the normal range but above the 40% cutoff for a clearly weak ventricle; clinicians call this mildly reduced.
An EF of {EF}% is normal: in each beat the ventricle ejects about {EF}% of what it holds and keeps the rest, {ESV} mL, as the end-systolic volume.
An EF of {EF}% is above the usual range. It can happen when the ventricle is strongly stimulated, or when its cavity is small and its wall thick, so little blood is left at the end of systole.
Notice that EF is normal here but SV is small: the ventricle is ejecting a normal share of a small filled volume. Low filling lowers stroke volume even when the ventricle contracts well.
Notice that SV is near normal even though EF is low: a ventricle that has enlarged holds more blood, so a small share of a big EDV can still be a normal-sized stroke volume.

asks.prompt: A ventricle holds {EDV} mL at the end of diastole and {ESV} mL at the end of systole. What is its ejection fraction, as a percentage?
An echocardiogram shows a left ventricle with an end-diastolic volume of {EDV} mL and an end-systolic volume of {ESV} mL. What is the stroke volume?

calculators.title: Pulse pressure
calculators.intro: Pulse pressure is how far arterial pressure swings with each beat: the systolic peak minus the diastolic low.
calculators.formula: PP = SBP − DBP

invalid.text: Diastolic pressure must be lower than systolic pressure: it is the lowest arterial pressure between beats.

steps.title: Subtract the low from the peak
steps.text: PP = SBP − DBP = {SBP} mm Hg − {DBP} mm Hg = {PP} mm Hg.

steps.title: Compare it with the systolic pressure
steps.text: A quarter of the systolic pressure is {quarter} mm Hg. A pulse pressure below that is called narrow; one above about 60 mm Hg is called wide.

results.label: Pulse pressure
results.normal: About 40 mm Hg in a healthy young adult at rest.

meaning.text: A narrow pulse pressure means each beat adds little pressure to the arteries. The usual reason is a small stroke volume, for example after heavy blood loss, or when a narrowed aortic valve lets blood out only slowly.

A wide pulse pressure means arterial pressure swings far with each beat. Two common causes: stiff arteries that cannot stretch to take up each stroke volume, which becomes common with age, or a larger stroke volume ejected more forcefully, as during exercise.
The {PP} mm Hg swing is the pressure each stroke volume adds as it stretches the elastic arteries. Elastic recoil of those walls then keeps pressure up between beats.

asks.prompt: A patient's blood pressure is {SBP}/{DBP} mm Hg. What is the pulse pressure?

calculators.title: Mean arterial pressure
calculators.intro: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is the average pressure in your arteries over a whole cardiac cycle, the pressure that drives blood through your tissues. From a cuff reading you can estimate it.
calculators.formula: MAP ≈ DBP + ⅓ × (SBP − DBP)

invalid.text: Diastolic pressure must be lower than systolic pressure: it is the lowest arterial pressure between beats.

steps.title: Find the pulse pressure
steps.text: PP = SBP − DBP = {SBP} mm Hg − {DBP} mm Hg = {PP} mm Hg.

steps.title: Take one third of it
steps.text: {PP} mm Hg ÷ 3 = {third} mm Hg.

steps.title: Add that to the diastolic pressure
steps.text: MAP ≈ DBP + ⅓ PP = {DBP} mm Hg + {third} mm Hg = {MAPx} mm Hg, or about {MAP} mm Hg.

steps.title: Why one third and not one half
steps.text: At a resting heart rate, diastole lasts about twice as long as systole, so the arteries spend about two-thirds of each cycle near diastolic pressure. The time-weighted average therefore sits one third of the way up from DBP. The simple average, (SBP + DBP) ÷ 2 = {avg} mm Hg, would overstate it.

results.label: Mean arterial pressure
results.normal: About 70 to 100 mm Hg in a resting adult. Below about 60 to 65 mm Hg, the brain, heart and kidneys may not get enough flow.

bands.label: too low for steady organ flow

meaning.text: A MAP of about {MAP} mm Hg is too low to keep enough blood flowing through the vessels of the brain, heart and kidneys. In emergency care, keeping MAP at about 65 mm Hg or above is a common target.

A MAP of about {MAP} mm Hg is below the usual resting range. Many people run low without harm, but a fall to this level from a higher baseline means less pressure is driving blood through the tissues.
A MAP of about {MAP} mm Hg is in the usual resting range. It is the average pressure pushing blood from the aorta, through the tissues, back toward the right atrium, where pressure is close to zero.
A MAP of about {MAP} mm Hg is high. The walls of the arteries and the left ventricle work against this higher pressure with every beat.

calculators.note: This is an estimate, and it assumes a resting heart rate. As heart rate rises, diastole shortens more than systole, so the arteries spend less time near diastolic pressure and the true mean moves toward the simple average. A monitor connected to a catheter in an artery measures MAP directly by averaging the whole pressure wave.

asks.prompt: A patient's blood pressure is {SBP}/{DBP} mm Hg and their heart rate is at rest. Estimate the mean arterial pressure to the nearest whole mm Hg.

calculators.title: Flow and resistance in vessels
calculators.intro: The flow equation applied to one organ: the pressure gradient across it is arterial pressure minus the pressure in its veins, and its resistance is set mostly by the radius of its arterioles. Change that radius and see what happens to the organ's blood flow.
calculators.formula: F = (MAP − P<sub>vein</sub>) ÷ R;  R ∝ 1 ÷ r<sup>4</sup>

inputs.label: Arteriole radius after the change, as a fraction of before

invalid.text: Venous pressure must be below arterial pressure, or there is no gradient to push blood through the organ.
The radius fraction must be greater than zero.

steps.title: Find the pressure gradient across the organ
steps.text: ΔP = MAP − P<sub>vein</sub> = {MAP} mm Hg − {Pv} mm Hg = {dP} mm Hg.

steps.title: Find the flow before the change
steps.text: F = ΔP ÷ R = {dP} mm Hg ÷ {R} mm Hg·min/L = {F0} L/min. The mm Hg cancel, leaving L/min.

steps.title: Find the new resistance
steps.text: Radius<sup>4</sup> changes by ({f})<sup>4</sup> = {f4}, so resistance changes by 1 ÷ {f4}: R = {R} ÷ {f4} = {R1} mm Hg·min/L.

steps.title: Find the new flow
steps.text: MAP is held steady by the rest of the circulation, so ΔP is still {dP} mm Hg. F = {dP} ÷ {R1} = {F1} L/min.

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: {F1} ÷ {F0} × 100 = {pct}% of the original flow.

meaning.text: Narrowing this organ's arterioles by only {narrow}% cut its blood flow to {pct}% of what it was, with no change in arterial pressure. Arterioles set most of an organ's resistance, and resistance varies with 1 ÷ radius<sup>4</sup>, so small changes in arteriole radius are how your body sends more blood to one organ and less to another.

Widening this organ's arterioles by only {widen}% raised its blood flow to {pct}% of what it was, with no change in arterial pressure. Vasodilation in one organ is how that organ draws more of the blood the heart pumps out.
With the arterioles unchanged, the organ's flow is set by its pressure gradient and resistance alone: {F0} L/min.

calculators.note: The organ values are round illustrations: at rest your kidneys receive about 1.1 L/min and your brain about 0.75 L/min.

asks.prompt: Mean arterial pressure is {MAP} mm Hg and the pressure in an organ's veins is {Pv} mm Hg. The organ's resistance is {R} mm Hg·min/L. Its arterioles then change to {f} times their original radius, while MAP and venous pressure stay the same. What is the organ's new blood flow?
Mean arterial pressure is {MAP} mm Hg and the pressure in an organ's veins is {Pv} mm Hg. The organ's vascular resistance is {R} mm Hg·min/L. What is the organ's blood flow?

calculators.title: Cardiac output
calculators.intro: Cardiac output (CO) is the volume of blood one ventricle pumps each minute: the number of beats per minute times the volume of each beat.
calculators.formula: CO = HR × SV

steps.title: Write the equation
steps.text: CO = HR × SV

steps.title: Substitute, keeping the units
steps.text: CO = {HR} beats/min × {SV} mL/beat

steps.title: Multiply, and let the beats cancel
steps.text: {HR} × {SV} = {COml}. Beats/min × mL/beat: the beats cancel, leaving {COml} mL/min.

steps.title: Convert to liters per minute
steps.text: {COml} mL/min ÷ 1,000 mL/L = {CO} L/min.

results.label: Cardiac output
results.normal: About 4 to 8 L/min in a resting adult, typically near 5.

meaning.text: A cardiac output of {CO} L/min is below the resting range: less blood reaches the tissues each minute. It can come from a slow heart rate, a small stroke volume, or both.
A cardiac output of {CO} L/min is in the resting range. Your blood volume is about 5 liters, so roughly all of it passes through each side of the heart every minute.

A cardiac output of {CO} L/min is above the resting range, as during exercise. The gap between resting and maximum output is the cardiac reserve: about 20 L/min is reachable in a young adult at peak effort.
At a heart rate this fast, filling time shortens, so the ventricles fill less and stroke volume usually falls. A faster heart does not always pump more.

asks.prompt: A person's heart rate is {HR} beats/min and each beat ejects {SV} mL. What is the cardiac output in liters per minute?
An echocardiogram measures a stroke volume of {SV} mL while the monitor shows a heart rate of {HR} beats/min. Calculate the cardiac output in L/min.

calculators.title: Net filtration pressure in a capillary
calculators.intro: Four Starling forces decide whether fluid moves out of a capillary or back in at one point along it. Enter the four pressures to find the net filtration pressure (NFP).
calculators.formula: NFP = (CHP + IFCOP) − (BCOP + IFHP)

inputs.label: Capillary hydrostatic pressure (pushes out)
inputs.hint: About 35 at the arteriole end, falling to about 15 at the venule end.

inputs.label: Interstitial fluid colloid osmotic pressure (pulls out)
Interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure (pushes in)
inputs.hint: Close to zero in most loose tissues.

steps.title: Add the forces that move fluid out
steps.text: CHP pushes out and IFCOP pulls out: {CHP} + {IFCOP} = {out} mm Hg outward.

steps.title: Add the forces that move fluid in
steps.text: BCOP pulls in and IFHP pushes in: {BCOP} + {IFHP:p} = {in} mm Hg inward.

steps.title: Subtract inward from outward
steps.text: NFP = {out} mm Hg − {in} mm Hg = {NFP:+} mm Hg.

steps.title: Read the sign
steps.text: A positive NFP favors filtration, fluid moving out of the capillary. A negative NFP favors reabsorption, fluid moving in. For a given capillary wall, the bigger the number, the faster fluid moves.

results.label: Net filtration pressure
results.normal: Classic textbook values give about +13 mm Hg at the arteriole end and about −7 mm Hg at the venule end.

meaning.text: With an NFP of {NFP:+} mm Hg, fluid filters out of the capillary into the interstitial fluid here. Plasma proteins stay behind. In most tissues, fluid filters out like this along almost the whole length of the capillary, and a separate drainage route carries it back to the blood.
The outward and inward forces balance, so there is no net fluid movement at this point.

An NFP of {NFP:+} mm Hg predicts reabsorption, fluid moving back into the capillary. In most tissues that inward flow lasts only minutes: as fluid flows in, proteins build up in the thin layer just beneath the glycocalyx, the inward pull weakens, and the flow fades. At steady state most capillaries keep filtering slowly all the way to the venule end (the revised Starling principle). Reabsorption continues only in a few special beds, such as the kidneys and the lining of the intestine. After a sudden fall in capillary pressure, as after blood loss, inward flow lasts only minutes; then the capillaries filter less than before while the drainage route keeps returning fluid, so the plasma keeps gaining fluid for hours.
BCOP is low here. With less plasma protein holding fluid in the blood, filtration speeds up at every point along the capillary; this is one cause of edema.
CHP is high here, as when venous pressure rises, for example after standing still for hours. More pressure pushes fluid out, and if filtration outpaces drainage, edema follows.

calculators.exam: Most textbooks and exams still teach the classic picture: net filtration at the arteriole end, net reabsorption at the venule end, with about 85 to 90 percent of the filtered fluid reabsorbed. If a question asks what happens at the venule end, answer "net reabsorption". The calculation here gives the same numbers; only the interpretation of a negative NFP differs.

asks.prompt: At one point along a capillary, CHP = {CHP} mm Hg, IFCOP = {IFCOP} mm Hg, BCOP = {BCOP} mm Hg and IFHP = {IFHP} mm Hg. What is the net filtration pressure? Give a negative value if it favors reabsorption.

calculators.title: Total peripheral resistance from MAP and cardiac output
calculators.intro: The flow equation for your whole systemic circuit gives MAP = CO × TPR. Rearranged, it tells you the total peripheral resistance (TPR) from a MAP and a cardiac output.
calculators.formula: TPR = MAP ÷ CO

invalid.text: Cardiac output must be greater than zero.

steps.title: Start from the flow equation
steps.text: For the whole systemic circuit, CO = (MAP − right atrial pressure) ÷ TPR. Right atrial pressure is close to 0 mm Hg, so CO ≈ MAP ÷ TPR, which rearranges to MAP = CO × TPR.

steps.title: Rearrange for TPR
steps.text: TPR = MAP ÷ CO

steps.title: Substitute, keeping the units
steps.text: TPR = {MAP} mm Hg ÷ {CO} L/min = {TPR} mm Hg·min/L.

steps.title: Check the units
steps.text: mm Hg divided by L/min gives mm Hg·min/L. Intensive care monitors often multiply by 80 to report the same value in dyn·s/cm<sup>5</sup>: {TPRd}.

results.label: Total peripheral resistance
results.normal: Roughly 10 to 20 mm Hg·min/L in a resting adult, typically near 18.

meaning.text: TPR is below the resting range: arterioles across the body are wider than usual, as in exercising muscle. MAP stays up only because cardiac output is high enough to match; if cardiac output did not rise, MAP would fall.
TPR is in the resting range. Most of it comes from the arterioles, whose radius is set moment to moment by sympathetic tone and local conditions.

TPR is above the resting range: arterioles across the body are narrower than usual, for example from strong sympathetic vasoconstriction. The heart must hold a higher arterial pressure to push the same cardiac output through them.

calculators.note: Ignoring right atrial pressure slightly overstates TPR. If right atrial pressure were 5 mm Hg, TPR would be ({MAP} − 5) ÷ {CO} = {TPRr} mm Hg·min/L.

asks.prompt: A person has a mean arterial pressure of {MAP} mm Hg and a cardiac output of {CO} L/min. Treating right atrial pressure as zero, what is their total peripheral resistance?

calculators.title: Boyle’s law: volume and pressure
calculators.intro: For a fixed amount of gas at a constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely related. Enter the starting pressure and volume and the new volume to find the new pressure, and how far it sits from the air outside.
calculators.formula: P₂ = P₁ × V₁ ÷ V₂

invalid.text: Volumes must be greater than zero.

steps.title: Write Boyle’s law
steps.text: P<sub>1</sub> × V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub> × V<sub>2</sub>. The same molecules in a larger space strike the walls less often, so pressure falls; in a smaller space, it rises.

steps.title: Rearrange for the new pressure
steps.text: Divide both sides by V<sub>2</sub>: P<sub>2</sub> = P<sub>1</sub> × V<sub>1</sub> ÷ V<sub>2</sub>.

steps.title: Substitute, with both volumes in the same unit
steps.text: P<sub>2</sub> = {P1} mm Hg × {V1} L ÷ {V2} L. The liters cancel, leaving mm Hg.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.text: {V1} ÷ {V2} = {ratio}; {P1} × {ratio} = {P2} mm Hg.

steps.title: Compare with the air outside
steps.text: {P2} − {P1} = {dP:+} mm Hg. Check the direction: a bigger volume must give a lower pressure, and a smaller volume a higher one.

results.label: New pressure
results.normal: At sea level the air outside is at 760 mm Hg. In a quiet breath, alveolar pressure swings only about 1 mm Hg either side of it.

meaning.text: The gas now sits {dP} mm Hg from where it started. If this is your alveolar air and the start was atmospheric pressure, air flows in through the airways until the pressures are equal again. That is inspiration.
The volume did not change, so neither did the pressure, and no gradient drives air in or out.

The gas now sits {dP:+} mm Hg above where it started. If this is your alveolar air and the start was atmospheric pressure, air flows out until the pressures are equal. Squeezed hard against closed vocal folds, as before a cough, the gradient becomes large.

presets.label: Start of a quiet breath in

asks.prompt: A sealed container holds {V1} L of air at {P1} mm Hg. Its volume changes to {V2} L at the same temperature. What is the new pressure?
A sealed bag of air at {P1} mm Hg is squeezed or stretched from {V1} L to {V2} L at the same temperature. What is the pressure inside it now?

calculators.title: Lung compliance
calculators.intro: Lung compliance is how much the lung volume changes for each mm Hg of change in transpulmonary pressure. Enter the volume breathed in and the transpulmonary pressure at the start and end of the breath.
calculators.formula: C = ΔV ÷ ΔP

invalid.text: For air to go in, transpulmonary pressure must rise during the breath, so the end value must be higher than the start.

steps.title: Find the change in pressure
steps.text: ΔP = {Pb} − {Pa} = {dP} mm Hg.

steps.title: Write the definition
steps.text: Compliance = ΔV ÷ ΔP: the volume gained for each mm Hg of pressure change.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: C = {dV} L ÷ {dP} mm Hg = {C} L/mm Hg.

steps.title: Compare with healthy lungs
steps.text: A healthy adult takes in 0.5 L for a 2 mm Hg rise: 0.25 L/mm Hg. 0.25 ÷ {C} = {times}, so these lungs need {times} times the pressure change of healthy ones for each liter.

results.label: Lung compliance
results.normal: About 0.25 L/mm Hg in healthy adult lungs during quiet breathing.

meaning.text: These lungs are stiff: each liter needs more pressure change, so the breathing muscles work harder on every breath. Scar tissue (fibrosis), fluid in the lung tissue, or too little surfactant all lower compliance.
Compliance is about normal: elastic fibers and surface tension, lowered by surfactant, resist stretch by the usual amount.
These lungs stretch unusually easily. That sounds helpful, but it usually means elastic fibers have been destroyed, so the lungs recoil weakly and breathing out becomes the hard part.

asks.prompt: During a breath in, transpulmonary pressure rises from {Pa} to {Pb} mm Hg and {dV} L of air enters. What is the lung compliance?

calculators.title: Lung capacities from lung volumes
calculators.intro: A capacity is the sum of two or more of the four lung volumes. Enter the four volumes to build the four capacities.
calculators.formula: IC = TV + IRV; FRC = ERV + RV; VC = TV + IRV + ERV; TLC = VC + RV

steps.title: Inspiratory capacity
steps.text: IC = TV + IRV = {TV} + {IRV} = {IC} mL: the most you can breathe in from the end of a quiet breath out.

steps.title: Functional residual capacity
steps.text: FRC = ERV + RV = {ERV} + {RV} = {FRC} mL: the air left in your lungs at the end of a quiet breath out.

steps.title: Vital capacity
steps.text: VC = TV + IRV + ERV = {TV} + {IRV} + {ERV} = {VC} mL: the most you can breathe out after the deepest breath in.

steps.title: Total lung capacity
steps.text: TLC = VC + RV = {VC} + {RV} = {TLC} mL.

steps.title: Check
steps.text: TLC should also equal IC + FRC: {IC} + {FRC} = {check} mL. Only IC and VC can be measured with a spirometer alone; FRC and TLC include the residual volume, which never passes the mouthpiece.

results.label: Vital capacity
results.normal: About 4,700 mL in a healthy young man; roughly 20 to 25% less in a woman of the same age.

results.label: Total lung capacity
results.normal: About 5,900 mL in a healthy young man.

results.label: Functional residual capacity
results.normal: About 2,400 mL.

results.label: Inspiratory capacity
results.normal: About 3,500 mL.

meaning.text: Residual volume is {rvpct}% of total lung capacity, a large share, as when narrowed airways close early and trap air. A larger residual volume leaves less room for the vital capacity.
Residual volume is {rvpct}% of total lung capacity. These values are typical of a healthy adult; real results are compared with values predicted for the person’s age, sex and height.

asks.prompt: A spirometry test gives a tidal volume of {TV} mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of {IRV} mL and an expiratory reserve volume of {ERV} mL. What is the vital capacity?
A patient has TV = {TV} mL, IRV = {IRV} mL and ERV = {ERV} mL, and a gas-dilution test finds a residual volume of {RV} mL. What is the total lung capacity?
A patient’s expiratory reserve volume is {ERV} mL and residual volume is {RV} mL. What is the functional residual capacity?

calculators.title: FEV1/FVC ratio
calculators.intro: In a forced breath out, FEV1 is the volume blown out in the first second and FVC the total. Their ratio shows how fast the lungs empty.
calculators.formula: ratio = FEV1 ÷ FVC

inputs.label: Volume blown out in the first second

invalid.text: FEV1 is part of the FVC, so it cannot be larger than it.

steps.title: Write the ratio
steps.text: FEV1/FVC = volume in the first second ÷ total volume.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.text: FEV1/FVC = {FEV1} L ÷ {FVC} L. The liters cancel: the ratio has no unit.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.text: {FEV1} ÷ {FVC} = {R}, so {pct}% of the air left in the first second.

steps.title: Compare with the cutoff
steps.text: Healthy young lungs empty about 80% in the first second (0.8). A ratio below about 0.70 means air is leaving too slowly.

results.label: FEV1/FVC
results.normal: About 0.8 in a young adult, falling a little with age.

meaning.text: A ratio of {R} means air leaves too slowly for the volume the person can move: an obstructive pattern. Narrowed airways, as in asthma, raise resistance and close early during the forced breath out.

A ratio of {R} is normal: the air leaves quickly. Whether an FVC of {FVC} L is small depends on the value predicted for the person’s age, sex and height. If it is well below predicted, small lungs that empty quickly suggest restriction, which only a measured total lung capacity can confirm.
A ratio of {R} is normal: the air leaves quickly. Compare the FVC with the value predicted for the person’s age, sex and height as well.

calculators.note: Many guidelines use the fixed cutoff of 0.70. Lung-function societies now prefer the lower limit of normal for the person’s age, sex and height, because the normal ratio falls with age.

asks.prompt: A patient blows out {FEV1} L in the first second of a forced breath out and {FVC} L in total. What is the FEV1/FVC ratio?

calculators.title: Minute and alveolar ventilation
calculators.intro: Minute ventilation is all the air moved each minute. Alveolar ventilation is the fresh air that reaches the alveoli, after the dead space is taken from every breath.
calculators.formula: Minute ventilation = TV × rate; alveolar ventilation = (TV − dead space) × rate

invalid.text: With a tidal volume no larger than the dead space, no fresh air reaches the alveoli at all: every breath only moves air back and forth in the conducting zone.

steps.title: Minute ventilation
steps.text: {TV} mL/breath × {RR} breaths/min = {VEml} mL/min = {VE} L/min. The breaths cancel.

steps.title: Fresh air per breath
steps.text: The last {VD} mL of each breath stops in the conducting zone, so {TV} − {VD} = {fresh} mL of fresh air reaches the alveoli.

steps.title: Alveolar ventilation
steps.text: {fresh} mL × {RR} breaths/min = {VAml} mL/min = {VA} L/min.

steps.title: Share wasted
steps.text: {VD} ÷ {TV} = {wasted}% of each breath is dead space.

results.label: Minute ventilation
results.normal: About 6 L/min at rest (12 breaths of 500 mL).

results.label: Alveolar ventilation
results.normal: About 4 to 5 L/min at rest.

meaning.text: Only {VA} L/min of fresh air reaches the alveoli, even though {VE} L/min moves in and out. Oxygen in the alveoli falls and carbon dioxide builds up, unless the body is using less oxygen than usual.
An alveolar ventilation of {VA} L/min is in the resting range: enough fresh air to hold the alveolar gases steady at rest.
An alveolar ventilation of {VA} L/min is above the resting range, as in exercise, when more oxygen is used and more carbon dioxide made.

Half or more of each breath is dead space. Fast, shallow breathing pays the fixed cost of the dead space on every breath; slower, deeper breaths deliver more fresh air for the same minute ventilation.

asks.prompt: A person breathes {RR} times a minute with a tidal volume of {TV} mL. The dead space is {VD} mL. What is the alveolar ventilation in L/min?
A patient takes {RR} breaths a minute, each of {TV} mL. What is the minute ventilation in L/min?

calculators.title: Partial pressure (Dalton’s law)
calculators.intro: Each gas in a mixture exerts its share of the total pressure. Enter the total air pressure, the water vapor pressure (47 mm Hg once air is warmed and moistened in your airways, 0 for dry air) and the oxygen percentage.
calculators.formula: PO₂ = (total pressure − water vapor pressure) × oxygen fraction

inputs.label: Water vapor pressure
inputs.hint: 47 in the airways at body temperature; 0 for dry air

invalid.text: The total pressure must be larger than the water vapor pressure.

steps.title: Subtract the water vapor
steps.text: The dry gases share what is left of the total: {P} − {W} = {Pdry} mm Hg.

steps.title: Turn the percentage into a fraction
steps.text: {F}% = {frac}.

steps.title: Take oxygen’s share
steps.text: PO2 = {Pdry} mm Hg × {frac} = {PO2} mm Hg.

steps.title: Compare with sea level
steps.text: Moist air breathed in at sea level has a PO<sub>2</sub> of about 149 mm Hg (713 × 0.209). This value is {seaPct}% of that.

results.label: Partial pressure of oxygen
results.normal: About 159 mm Hg in dry air and about 150 in warmed, moistened air at sea level.

meaning.text: A PO<sub>2</sub> of {PO2} mm Hg pushes oxygen into the blood with less force than at sea level, even when the air is still 20.9% oxygen. The total pressure, not the percentage, is what has fallen.
A PO<sub>2</sub> of {PO2} mm Hg is about what you breathe at sea level. After mixing with the air already in the alveoli, it falls to about 100 mm Hg.
A PO<sub>2</sub> of {PO2} mm Hg is above sea-level air, from a higher oxygen fraction or a higher total pressure, as in a hyperbaric chamber. By Henry’s law, more oxygen dissolves in the plasma.

asks.prompt: The total air pressure is {P} mm Hg and the water vapor pressure is {W} mm Hg. The dry gas is {F}% oxygen. What is the PO2?

calculators.title: Oxygen content of blood
calculators.intro: Blood carries oxygen bound to hemoglobin and dissolved in plasma. Enter the hemoglobin concentration, the saturation and the PO2 to find how much oxygen 100 mL of blood carries.
calculators.formula: O₂ content = 1.34 × Hb × saturation + 0.003 × PO₂

steps.title: Bound to hemoglobin
steps.text: Each gram of fully loaded hemoglobin carries 1.34 mL of oxygen: 1.34 × {Hb} × {S}% = {bound} mL per 100 mL.

steps.title: Dissolved in plasma (Henry’s law)
steps.text: 0.003 mL per 100 mL for each mm Hg: 0.003 × {PO2} = {diss} mL per 100 mL.

steps.title: Add them
steps.text: {bound} + {diss} = {total} mL of oxygen per 100 mL of blood. Hemoglobin carries {share}% of it.

results.label: Oxygen content
results.normal: About 20 mL per 100 mL in arterial blood and about 15 in venous blood at rest.

meaning.text: At this low PO2 and saturation, the blood has already given up much of its oxygen, as in venous blood or on the steep part of the dissociation curve. About {total} mL per 100 mL remains.
Only {total} mL per 100 mL. With a normal saturation, the likely cause is too little hemoglobin (anemia) or hemoglobin blocked by carbon monoxide. Saturation alone would look normal.
About {total} mL per 100 mL, a normal arterial content. Resting tissues take only about a quarter of it; the rest is a reserve.
{total} mL per 100 mL is above the usual range, from a high hemoglobin, as after weeks at high altitude.

asks.prompt: A blood sample has {Hb} g of hemoglobin per 100 mL, a saturation of {S}% and a PO2 of {PO2} mm Hg. How much oxygen does 100 mL carry? (1.34 mL per g of hemoglobin; 0.003 mL per 100 mL per mm Hg dissolved.)

calculators.title: Alveolar ventilation and PCO2
calculators.intro: When carbon dioxide production stays the same, arterial PCO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation. Enter the starting PCO2 and alveolar ventilation, and the new alveolar ventilation.
calculators.formula: PCO₂(new) = PCO₂(old) × V̇A(old) ÷ V̇A(new)

steps.title: Write the relationship
steps.text: With carbon dioxide production constant, PCO<sub>2</sub> × alveolar ventilation stays the same: {P1} × {VA1} = {k}.

steps.title: How much has ventilation changed?
steps.text: {VA2} ÷ {VA1} = {fold} times the starting ventilation.

steps.title: Divide the constant by the new ventilation
steps.text: PCO2 = {k} ÷ {VA2} = {P2} mm Hg.

steps.title: Link to pH
steps.text: A lower PCO<sub>2</sub> means fewer hydrogen ions and a higher pH; a higher PCO<sub>2</sub> the opposite.

results.label: New arterial PCO2
results.normal: Normal arterial PCO2 is 35 to 45 mm Hg.

meaning.text: A PCO<sub>2</sub> of {P2} mm Hg is hypocapnia: the person is hyperventilating, breathing more than carbon dioxide production requires. Blood pH rises.
A PCO<sub>2</sub> of {P2} mm Hg is in the normal range. Chemoreceptors hold it near 40 by adjusting ventilation.
A PCO<sub>2</sub> of {P2} mm Hg is hypercapnia: the person is hypoventilating, and blood pH falls.

asks.prompt: A resting adult has an arterial PCO2 of {P1} mm Hg with an alveolar ventilation of {VA1} L/min. Carbon dioxide production stays the same while alveolar ventilation changes to {VA2} L/min. What will arterial PCO2 settle at?

calculators.title: Time for a cut nerve to regrow
calculators.intro: After a nerve is cut and repaired, its axons regrow along Schwann cell tubes at about 1 mm a day. Dividing the distance still to grow by that rate estimates how long feeling or movement takes to return.
calculators.formula: Time (days) = distance (mm) ÷ regrowth rate (mm/day)

inputs.label: Distance from the repair to the target

steps.title: Put the distance in the rate’s unit
steps.text: {d} cm × 10 mm/cm = {mm} mm.

steps.title: Divide by the rate
steps.text: Time = {mm} mm ÷ {r} mm/day = {days} days.

steps.title: Convert to months
steps.text: {days} days ÷ 30 days per month ≈ {months} months.

results.label: Regrowth time
results.normal: Feeling returns first near the repair and last at the far end.

meaning.text: Over a year of regrowth is a real risk: muscle fibers without a nerve supply waste away before the axon arrives, and sprouts may stray into the wrong tubes. That is why surgeons repair nerves quickly and line the ends up precisely.
This is a minimum. The sprouts need days to weeks to cross the repair site before steady growth begins, so real recovery takes somewhat longer, and it moves outward from the scar toward the target.

presets.label: Worked example: 20 cm to the fingertip
Cut high in the arm: 60 cm

asks.prompt: A nerve is repaired {d} cm from the muscle it supplies. Its axons regrow at {r} mm/day. About how many days until they reach the muscle?

calculators.title: Conduction time along an axon
calculators.intro: An action potential travels along an axon at its conduction velocity, from about 0.5 m/s in thin unmyelinated axons to about 120 m/s in wide myelinated ones. Dividing the distance by the velocity gives the time it takes to arrive.
calculators.formula: Time (s) = distance (m) ÷ conduction velocity (m/s)

steps.title: Write the relationship
steps.text: Time = distance ÷ velocity.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.text: Time = {d} m ÷ {v} m/s = {t} s.

results.label: Conduction time
results.normal: About 20 ms for 1 m on a myelinated touch fiber at 50 m/s; about 1,000 ms for 1 m on an unmyelinated fiber at 1 m/s.

meaning.text: A velocity of {v} m/s is typical of a thin unmyelinated axon, where every patch of membrane fires in turn (continuous conduction). Slow, dull, aching pain travels on fibers like this, so it arrives well after the sharp first sensation.
A velocity of {v} m/s needs myelin: the action potential is regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction). Wider axons conduct faster still.
At {v} m/s the axon is slower than healthy myelinated fibers, as a demyelinated axon that has added sodium channels along its bare stretch might be.

presets.label: Touch, foot to spinal cord: 1 m at 50 m/s
Dull pain, same distance: 1 m at 1 m/s
Fastest motor axon: 1 m at 120 m/s

asks.prompt: A signal travels {d} m along an axon that conducts at {v} m/s. How many milliseconds does it take?

calculators.title: Highest possible firing rate
calculators.intro: No second action potential can start during the absolute refractory period, so two spikes can be no closer together than that period. Its length sets the ceiling on how many action potentials a neuron can fire each second.
calculators.formula: Maximum rate (per s) = 1 s ÷ absolute refractory period (s)

steps.title: Find the shortest gap between spikes
steps.text: A new spike cannot start until the absolute refractory period ends, so the shortest gap is {arp} ms.

steps.title: Convert to seconds
steps.text: {arp} ms = {s} s.

steps.title: Count the gaps in one second
steps.text: 1 s ÷ {s} s = {rate} action potentials per second.

results.label: Ceiling on firing rate
results.normal: An absolute refractory period of about 1 to 2 ms caps firing at about 500 to 1,000 per second.

meaning.text: This is a ceiling, not a typical rate. A spike fired during the relative refractory period needs a stronger-than-normal stimulus, so real neurons fire below {rate} per second. Within that limit, a stronger stimulus raises the firing rate, not the size of each spike.

asks.prompt: A neuron’s absolute refractory period is {arp} ms. What is the highest rate, in action potentials per second, at which it could possibly fire?

calculators.title: Will the neuron fire? Summing EPSPs and IPSPs
calculators.intro: Postsynaptic potentials arriving together add algebraically at the trigger zone: EPSPs push toward threshold and IPSPs pull away. If the sum reaches threshold, the neuron fires.
calculators.formula: Potential at trigger zone = rest + (number of EPSPs × EPSP size) − (number of IPSPs × IPSP size)

invalid.text: Threshold must be above (less negative than) the resting potential.

steps.title: Find the depolarization needed
steps.text: Threshold − rest = {thr} − ({rest}) = {need} mV.

steps.title: Add the inputs
steps.text: EPSPs: {ne} × {e} mV = +{up} mV. IPSPs: {ni} × {i} mV = −{down} mV. Net = {net:+} mV.

steps.title: Find the potential at the trigger zone
steps.text: {rest} mV + ({net:+} mV) = {vm} mV.

steps.title: Compare with threshold
steps.text: Threshold is {thr} mV, so the membrane is {short} mV short of it (a zero or negative number means it has reached threshold).

results.label: Potential at the trigger zone
results.normal: The neuron fires if this reaches threshold.

meaning.text: The sum reaches threshold, so an action potential fires. If the inputs keep arriving, the trigger zone fires again as soon as each refractory period allows, and stronger combined input means a higher firing rate.
Inhibition outweighs excitation, so the trigger zone is pulled below rest, further from threshold than when the neuron is idle.

The sum falls {short} mV short of threshold. The graded potentials fade and no action potential fires. More simultaneous EPSPs (spatial summation), faster repeats (temporal summation) or fewer IPSPs would be needed.

presets.label: Worked example: 3 EPSPs of 4 mV, 1 IPSP of 3 mV
Five EPSPs with the same IPSP

asks.prompt: A neuron rests at {rest} mV with threshold at {thr} mV. At the same moment, {ne} excitatory inputs each give an EPSP of {e} mV and {ni} inhibitory inputs each give an IPSP of {i} mV. What potential does the trigger zone reach, in mV?

calculators.title: How long a reflex takes
calculators.intro: A reflex’s delay is the time the signal spends in the sensory axon, at the synapses of the integration center, in the motor axon, and at the neuromuscular junction as the muscle starts to contract. Axon time is distance divided by conduction velocity.
calculators.formula: Delay (ms) = sensory length ÷ sensory velocity + motor length ÷ motor velocity + about 1 ms per central synapse + about 3 ms for the junction and the start of contraction

inputs.label: Synapses in the integration center
inputs.hint: 1 for a stretch reflex; more when interneurons are involved

steps.title: Time in the sensory axon
steps.text: Time = distance ÷ speed = {ls} m ÷ {vs} m/s, then × 1000 to convert seconds to milliseconds = {ts} ms.

steps.title: Add the central synapses
steps.text: {n} synapse(s) × about 1 ms = {n} ms (about 0.5 ms of synaptic delay, plus the time the next neuron takes to reach threshold).

steps.title: Add the junction and the muscle
steps.text: Neuromuscular junction and the start of contraction: about 3 ms.

steps.title: Total
steps.text: {ts} + {tm} + {n} + 3 = {total} ms. The axons account for about {share}% of it.

results.label: Reflex delay
results.normal: About 20 to 25 ms for a knee jerk in an adult; longer for a reflex with more synapses or a longer path.

meaning.text: A velocity under 30 m/s is far below the 50 to 80 m/s of healthy large myelinated axons. In a stretch reflex that points to disease, as when myelin is stripped from peripheral nerves: the delay grows, and because the burst of signals arrives spread out in time, the reflex also weakens. (Healthy thin pain axons are this slow, which is one reason a withdrawal reflex takes longer.)
With {n} synapses the reflex is polysynaptic. Each extra synapse adds only about a millisecond, but interneurons let one input reach many motor neurons, as in the withdrawal reflex.

A single synapse makes this a monosynaptic stretch reflex, the fastest reflex you have. About {share}% of the {total} ms is spent in the axons, so conduction speed, not the synapse, sets most of the delay.

calculators.note: The synapse and muscle times are typical round figures. Each extra central synapse adds roughly half a millisecond to a millisecond.

presets.label: Worked example: knee jerk, 0.6 m each way
Ankle jerk in a tall adult: 1.0 m each way
Knee jerk with demyelinated nerves: 20 m/s

asks.prompt: In a reflex arc, the sensory path is {ls} m long and conducts at {vs} m/s, and the motor path is {lm} m long and conducts at {vm} m/s. There are {n} central synapse(s) at about 1 ms each, and the junction and start of contraction add 3 ms. What is the total delay, in ms?

calculators.title: Glasgow Coma Scale total
calculators.intro: The Glasgow Coma Scale scores the best response in three categories: eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5) and motor response (1 to 6). The total runs from 3 to 15. Report the parts as well as the total.
calculators.formula: GCS = eye opening score E + verbal score V + motor score M

inputs.label: Eye opening
inputs.hint: 4 spontaneously, 3 to sound, 2 to pressure, 1 none

inputs.label: Verbal response
inputs.hint: 5 oriented, 4 confused, 3 inappropriate words, 2 incomprehensible sounds, 1 none

inputs.label: Motor response
inputs.hint: 6 obeys, 5 localizes, 4 normal flexion, 3 abnormal flexion, 2 extension, 1 none

steps.title: Score each category
steps.text: Eyes E{e}, verbal V{v}, motor M{m}: always the best response seen.

steps.title: Report it
steps.text: GCS {total} (E{e} V{v} M{m}). The parts matter because the same total can hide very different patients.

results.label: GCS total
results.normal: 15 in a fully awake, oriented person who obeys commands.

meaning.text: GCS 15: eyes open on their own, oriented speech and obeying commands, the best score possible.
GCS {total} is in the mild range (13 to 15).
GCS {total} is in the moderate range (9 to 12). Consciousness is clearly impaired, and the trend over time matters as much as the number.
GCS {total} is in the severe range (8 or less), the usual working definition of coma. A person this impaired may not be able to protect their own airway.

calculators.exam: Many EMS and nursing exams teach “GCS 8, intubate.” Treat a total of 8 or less as a prompt to assess the airway, not a rule on its own.

presets.label: Same patient, bending away from pressure: E2 V3 M4
No response at all: E1 V1 M1

asks.prompt: After a head injury, a patient scores E{e} for eye opening, V{v} for verbal response and M{m} for motor response. What is the GCS total?

calculators.title: Reading a Snellen fraction
calculators.intro: Visual acuity is written as a fraction. The top number is your distance from the chart; the bottom is the distance at which a normal eye can just read the smallest row you read. Dividing the bottom by the top tells you how many times larger your letters must be than a normal eye needs.
calculators.formula: Size factor = row distance (bottom number) ÷ test distance (top number)

inputs.label: Label of the smallest row you can read

steps.title: Write the fraction
steps.text: Top: your distance, {d} ft. Bottom: the smallest row you read, {r}. Acuity = {d}/{r}.

steps.title: Compare the distances
steps.text: A normal eye could read that row from {r} ft; you must be at {d} ft.

steps.title: Find the size factor
steps.text: {r} ÷ {d} = {f}: your letters must be {f} times as large as a normal eye needs.

results.label: Size factor
results.normal: 1: a normal eye (20/20). Many young adults see better than that, around 20/15.

meaning.text: {d}/{r} is better than normal: you read from {d} ft what a normal eye must come to {r} ft to read.
{d}/{r} is normal acuity.
{d}/{r} means letters must be {f} times as large as normal. In the United States, a best-corrected acuity of 20/200 or worse in the better eye is one definition of legal blindness.

{d}/{r} is worse than normal: letters must be {f} times as large as a normal eye needs. The larger the bottom number, the worse the acuity. If it is a focusing error, the right lenses usually restore it.

presets.label: Worked example: Priya reads the 40 row
Only the top letter: the 200 row

asks.prompt: Standing {d} ft from a Snellen chart, a patient can read the row labeled {r} but no smaller. How many times as large as a normal eye needs must his letters be?

calculators.title: How the middle ear boosts pressure
calculators.intro: Sound must pass from air into the fluid of the cochlea, and most of it would bounce off. The middle ear raises the pressure in two ways: the force collected over the large eardrum is delivered onto the small stapes footplate (pressure = force ÷ area), and the ossicles act as a lever that adds a little force.
calculators.formula: Pressure gain = (eardrum area ÷ footplate area) × lever ratio of the ossicles

inputs.label: Vibrating area of the tympanic membrane

steps.title: Area ratio
steps.text: The same force spread over the eardrum is delivered to the footplate: {ad} mm² ÷ {af} mm² = {area}. Pressure = force ÷ area, so pressure rises {area}-fold.

steps.title: Lever
steps.text: The malleus is a little longer than the arm of the incus it pushes, multiplying the force by {lv}.

steps.title: Combine
steps.text: {area} × {lv} = {gain}: the pressure at the oval window is about {gain} times the pressure on the eardrum.

results.label: Pressure gain
results.normal: Roughly 20-fold in a healthy middle ear.

meaning.text: A gain of only {gain} would deliver much less pressure to the cochlea’s fluid, and more sound would be reflected, as it is at the surface of a swimming pool.

A gain of about {gain} is what lets sound in air move the fluid of the cochlea. Almost all of it comes from the area ratio; the lever adds the rest. When the ossicles cannot move freely, as with fluid in the middle ear or a stapes fused in the oval window, this boost is lost: a conductive hearing loss.

presets.label: A torn eardrum vibrating over only 30 mm²

asks.prompt: An eardrum vibrates over {ad} mm², the stapes footplate is {af} mm², and the ossicles act as a lever with a ratio of {lv}. By what factor does the middle ear raise the pressure?

calculators.title: Decibels and sound intensity
calculators.intro: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB) on a logarithmic scale: every 10 dB step is a tenfold rise in sound intensity. So the difference between two sounds in decibels tells you how many times more intense one is than the other.
calculators.formula: Intensity ratio = 10^(difference in dB ÷ 10)

invalid.text: Enter the louder sound second.

steps.title: Find the difference
steps.text: {l2} dB − {l1} dB = {diff} dB.

steps.title: Count 10 dB steps
steps.text: {diff} ÷ 10 = {steps10} steps, each a tenfold rise.

steps.title: Convert to a ratio
steps.text: 10^{steps10} = {ratio}: the louder sound is {ratio} times as intense.

results.label: Intensity ratio
results.normal: Normal conversation is about 60 dB. Hours above about 85 dB can damage hair cells.

meaning.text: At {l2} dB the louder sound is {ratio} times as intense as the quieter one. Hours at about 85 dB can destroy hair cells, and the safe time shrinks fast as the level rises: at 100 to 110 dB, minutes are enough. Outer hair cells near the base of the cochlea go first, and humans cannot replace them.
A difference of {diff} dB means {ratio} times the intensity. Because the scale is logarithmic, a sound that seems only somewhat louder can carry many times more energy.

presets.label: Conversation (60 dB) vs a busy workshop (90 dB)
Conversation vs the 85 dB risk level
Whisper (30 dB) vs loud music (110 dB)

asks.prompt: One sound measures {l1} dB and another {l2} dB. How many times as intense is the louder one?

calculators.title: Hematocrit from a spun tube
calculators.intro: After spinning, the packed red cells sit at the bottom of the tube. The hematocrit is the share of the blood column they fill.
calculators.formula: Hct = (height of red column ÷ height of whole blood column) × 100%

inputs.label: Height of the whole blood column (bottom of red cells to top of plasma)

invalid.text: The red column must be shorter than the whole blood column: plasma always sits on top of it.

steps.title: Write the definition
steps.text: Hematocrit = height of the red column ÷ height of the whole blood column × 100%.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: {R} mm ÷ {T} mm = {frac}.

steps.title: Convert to a percentage
steps.text: {frac} × 100% = {H}%. The rest, {P}%, is plasma plus a buffy coat of well under 1%.

results.label: Hematocrit
results.normal: About 37–47% in women and 42–52% in men; each laboratory sets its own range.

bands.label: in range for one sex only

meaning.text: Red cells fill less of the blood than usual. Either the red cell volume has fallen (fewer red cells), or plasma volume has risen and diluted them, as after a large volume of fluid through a drip.

Red cells fill more of the blood than usual. Either there are more red cells, or plasma water has been lost, as in dehydration, which raises the share without adding a single cell. More red cells also make the blood more viscous.
A hematocrit of {H}% is in range for one sex but not the other: below 42% is low for a man, and above 47% is high for a woman. Always compare with the range for the patient’s sex.
A hematocrit of {H}% is typical. Remember it is a ratio: right after a sudden bleed, cells and plasma are lost together, so the hematocrit is unchanged until fluid moves in and dilutes the cells.

asks.prompt: A spun tube has a red column {R} mm tall and a whole blood column {T} mm tall. What is the hematocrit?

calculators.title: Red cell and plasma volume
calculators.short: RCV = BV × Hct; PV = BV − RCV
calculators.intro: Blood is about 70 mL per kilogram of body weight. The hematocrit splits that volume into red cells and plasma.
calculators.formula: BV = 70 mL/kg × mass;  RCV = BV × Hct;  PV = BV − RCV

steps.title: Estimate the blood volume
steps.text: Blood volume ≈ 70 mL/kg × {M} kg = {BV} L.

steps.title: Red cell volume
steps.text: Red cells are {H}% of that: {BV} L × {H} ÷ 100 = {RCV} L.

steps.title: Plasma volume
steps.text: The rest is plasma (the buffy coat is too small to matter): {BV} − {RCV} = {PV} L.

steps.title: Check
steps.text: {PV} ÷ {BV} should be {PP}%, which is 100% − {H}%.

results.label: Red cell volume
results.normal: About 2.25 L in a 70 kg adult with a hematocrit of 45%.

results.label: Plasma volume
results.normal: About 2.75 L in a 70 kg adult with a hematocrit of 45%.

meaning.text: With a low hematocrit, a larger share of the {BV} L is plasma. The same total volume carries less oxygen, because oxygen rides on the red cells.
About {RCV} L of this person’s {BV} L of blood is red cells and {PV} L is plasma. The 70 mL/kg rule is an estimate; men average 5–6 L and women 4–5 L, mostly because of body size.

asks.prompt: A {M} kg adult has a hematocrit of {H}%. Using 70 mL of blood per kilogram, estimate the plasma volume.

calculators.title: How many red cells the marrow makes
calculators.short: made per day = red cells ÷ lifespan
calculators.intro: When the red cell count is steady, the marrow must make as many cells each day as are destroyed. That rate follows from the number of red cells and how long each one lasts.
calculators.formula: made per day = total red cells ÷ lifespan in days;  per second = per day ÷ 86,400

inputs.label: Total red cells in the body

steps.title: Assume a steady state
steps.text: If the count is not changing, cells made each day = cells destroyed each day. Each day, 1/{L} of the cells are replaced.

steps.title: Per day
steps.text: {N} trillion ÷ {L} days = {N} × 1,000 billion ÷ {L} = {D} billion cells per day.

steps.title: Per second
steps.text: A day has 86,400 seconds. {D} billion ÷ 86,400 = {S} million cells per second.

steps.title: Check with the reticulocytes
steps.text: 1/{L} of the cells is {F}% a day. Each new cell spends about a day in the blood as a reticulocyte, so reticulocytes should be about {F}% of red cells.

results.label: Red cells made each day
results.normal: About 210 billion a day in an adult with 25 trillion red cells that live 120 days.

meaning.text: A lifespan of {L} days means cells are destroyed early, as in hemolytic anemias. To hold the count steady, the marrow must work faster than usual, and the reticulocyte count rises to show it. If destruction outpaces the marrow’s best effort, the count falls.
At {L} days per cell, the marrow must make about {D} billion red cells a day, {S} million a second, just to stand still.

asks.prompt: An adult has {N} trillion red cells, each lasting {L} days, and the count is steady. How many billion red cells must the marrow make each day?

calculators.title: Absolute neutrophil count
calculators.intro: A differential gives each white cell type as a percentage. Multiply by the total white count to get how many of that type are really there: the absolute count.
calculators.formula: Absolute count = total white count × (percentage ÷ 100)

steps.title: Write the rule
steps.text: Absolute count = total white cell count × fraction of that type.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.text: {W} × {f} = {A} neutrophils per µL.

steps.title: Compare with normal
steps.text: A normal absolute neutrophil count is roughly 1,800–7,700 per µL. Below 500 per µL, the risk of a serious bacterial infection is very high.

results.label: Absolute neutrophil count
results.normal: Roughly 1,800–7,700 per µL.

meaning.text: Severe neutropenia. Neutrophils are the first defense against bacteria, so this patient needs precautions against infection; after chemotherapy, a colony-stimulating factor may be given to speed the marrow’s recovery.
Fewer neutrophils than normal: causes include chemotherapy, some viral infections, some drugs and marrow failure.
More neutrophils than normal, the typical pattern of a bacterial infection. The other types’ percentages fall even if their absolute counts do not, so check each one’s absolute count too.
An absolute neutrophil count of {A} per µL is within the normal range. A percentage alone can mislead: always multiply by the total.

asks.prompt: A patient’s white cell count is {W} per µL, and {P}% of the white cells are neutrophils. What is the absolute neutrophil count?

calculators.title: Hormone clearance and half-life
calculators.intro: When a gland stops secreting, the hormone already in the blood is cleared at a steady fractional rate. The half-life is the time for half of it to go. Enter the starting level, the half-life and the time since secretion stopped.
calculators.formula: Level after time t = starting level × (1/2)<sup>n</sup>, where n = t ÷ half-life

inputs.label: Half-life
inputs.hint: epinephrine about 2 min; most peptides a few minutes; the thyroid gland’s main hormone about a week (10,080 min)

steps.title: Count the half-lives
steps.text: n = {t} min ÷ {h} min per half-life = {n} half-lives.

steps.title: Find the fraction left
steps.text: Each half-life halves what is left, so the fraction left is (1/2){n} = {frac}, which is {pct}%.

steps.title: Multiply by the starting level
steps.text: Level = {L0} × {frac} = {L} units.

steps.title: Check by halving
steps.text: When n is a whole number you can halve step by step: {L0}, then half of that once per half-life, until you have halved n times.

results.label: Level left in the blood
results.normal: After 1 half-life, 50% is left; after 2, 25%; after 3, 12.5%; after 5, about 3%.

meaning.text: After about five half-lives, less than 5% is left, and the hormone’s effect has essentially gone. A hormone with a half-life of minutes, like epinephrine, is gone within a quarter of an hour of the gland stopping.

Less than one half-life has passed, so more than half of the hormone is still in the blood. A hormone with a long half-life, like the thyroid gland’s main hormone (about a week), lingers for weeks after its gland stops.
{pct}% of the starting level is left. The shorter the half-life, the faster the level follows the gland: short half-lives suit signals that must switch off quickly.

presets.label: Worked example: 80 units, half-life 10 min, 30 min later
The thyroid gland’s main hormone: half-life 1 week (10,080 min), 1 week later

practice.require: round(t / h) == t / h && t / h <= 5

calculators.title: Free and bound hormone
calculators.intro: A lipid-soluble hormone rides mostly on carrier proteins. Only the free part can leave the capillaries and bind receptor proteins, so the free level is what acts. Enter the total level and the percentage bound; add a second percentage to see what a change in binding does.
calculators.formula: Free hormone = total × (100 − percent bound) ÷ 100

invalid.text: Some hormone is always free, so the percent bound must be below 100.

steps.title: Free hormone before
steps.text: {f1pct}% of {T} = {f1pct} ÷ 100 × {T} = {f1} units.

steps.title: Free hormone after
steps.text: {f2pct}% of {T} = {f2} units, if the total has not yet changed.

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: Free hormone changes by a factor of {f2pct} ÷ {f1pct} = {ratio}, although the percent bound moved only from {b1}% to {b2}%.

meaning.text: Free hormone rises by a factor of {ratio}. Because the free share is small, a few percent less binding makes a big difference to the active hormone. Over the following hours the extra free hormone is cleared faster and, through negative feedback, the gland slows, so the free level drifts back toward normal.
Free hormone falls to {ratio} times its old level. More binding locks more hormone in the reservoir, so less reaches the target cells until the gland makes up the difference.
The free level has barely changed, so the target cells see about the same amount of active hormone.

presets.label: The thyroid gland’s hormones: over 99% bound
A steroid that is about 90% bound

asks.prompt: A hormone’s total level is {T} units and {b1}% is bound. A drug displaces some of it, so only {b2}% is bound and the total has not yet changed. What is the free level now?

calculators.title: Blood glucose units: mmol/L to mg/dL
calculators.intro: Most of the world reports blood glucose in mmol/L; the United States uses mg/dL. One mole of glucose weighs 180 g, so 1 mmol/L is 180 mg in 10 dL: 18 mg/dL. Enter a reading in mmol/L.
calculators.formula: Glucose (mg/dL) = glucose (mmol/L) × 18

steps.title: Find the conversion factor
steps.text: 1 mmol of glucose weighs 180 mg, and a liter is 10 dL, so 1 mmol/L = 180 mg ÷ 10 dL = 18 mg/dL.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.text: {mm} mmol/L × 18 = {mg} mg/dL.

steps.title: Going the other way
steps.text: To turn mg/dL into mmol/L, divide by 18: {mg} ÷ 18 = {mm} mmol/L.

results.label: Glucose
results.normal: Fasting: about 70–99 mg/dL (3.9–5.5 mmol/L). After a meal it usually peaks below 140.

bands.label: at or above the fasting cutoff for diabetes

meaning.text: {mg} mg/dL is below 54, clinically important hypoglycemia whatever the symptoms. The brain, which depends on blood glucose minute by minute, is running short.
{mg} mg/dL is hypoglycemia. Glucagon and epinephrine rise, and a conscious person should take about 15 g of fast sugar and recheck after 15 minutes.
{mg} mg/dL is inside the normal fasting range.
{mg} mg/dL is above the normal fasting range but below the diagnostic cutoff. After a meal, values up to about 140 are normal.

{mg} mg/dL. If this was a fasting reading, and a repeat on another day is also 126 or more, it meets the diagnostic cutoff for diabetes. Random readings of 200 or more with the classic symptoms also qualify.

asks.prompt: A glucose meter reads {mm} mmol/L. What is that in mg/dL?

calculators.title: Folds, villi and microvilli: how much surface?
calculators.intro: Each level of folding in the small intestine multiplies the surface made by the level before it, so the factors multiply. Textbooks often use about 3 for circular folds, 10 for villi and 20 for microvilli. Direct measurements give smaller factors (about 1.6 for the folds and 60 to 120 for villi and microvilli together), so the real total is roughly 100- to 200-fold. Enter a factor for each level.
calculators.formula: Total amplification = circular folds × villi × microvilli

inputs.label: Circular folds multiply the surface by

steps.title: Start with a smooth tube
steps.text: Call the inner surface of a smooth tube of the same length and width 1.

steps.title: Circular folds
steps.text: 1 × {f} = {f}. The folds of the mucosa and submucosa multiply the smooth surface.

steps.title: Villi on the folds
steps.text: {f} × {v} = {fv}. Villi cover the whole mucosa, folds included, so their factor multiplies the folded surface.

steps.title: Microvilli on every absorptive cell
steps.text: {fv} × {m} = {total}. Microvilli cover every absorptive cell on every villus, so their factor multiplies again.

steps.title: Compare with the textbook estimate
steps.text: {total} ÷ 600 = {share}% of the textbook total of 3 × 10 × 20 = 600.

results.label: Total surface amplification
results.normal: Measured in living people: roughly 100- to 200-fold (about 30 m² in all). Textbook estimate: about 600-fold.

bands.label: about the textbook estimate or above

meaning.text: With the villus factor at 1, the villi are flattened, as happens when an immune reaction to gluten (celiac disease) damages the lining. The surface is {total}-fold, and absorption falls roughly in proportion, which is why people lose weight and develop deficiencies even when they eat enough.
A {total}-fold surface is well below the roughly 100- to 200-fold measured in healthy people. Absorption falls roughly in proportion to the lost surface.
A {total}-fold surface is about what direct measurements find: the small intestine’s lining covers roughly 30 m², about 15 to 20 times the area of your skin.

A {total}-fold surface is about the textbook estimate of 600-fold, which older books turned into "a tennis court" (200 to 300 m²). Measurements in living people give about 30 m². For an exam, the textbook figures may still be expected.

asks.prompt: Circular folds multiply the surface by {f}, villi by {v} and microvilli by {m}. By how much do they multiply it together?

calculators.title: Emulsification: how much surface for lipase?
calculators.short: surface gain = large diameter ÷ small diameter
calculators.intro: Bile salts keep churned fat in tiny droplets. Lipase works only at a droplet’s surface, so what matters is how much surface the same volume of fat offers. Enter the diameter of a large droplet and of the small droplets it is broken into.
calculators.formula: Surface gain = D ÷ d (number of droplets = (D ÷ d)³; area of each = 1 ÷ (D ÷ d)²)

invalid.text: The small droplets must be smaller than the large one.

steps.title: How many times smaller?
steps.text: {D} mm ÷ {d} mm = {r}. Each small droplet is {r} times narrower.

steps.title: Count the new droplets
steps.text: Volume scales with diameter cubed, so each small droplet has {r}³ = {n} times less volume. The same fat makes {n} small droplets.

steps.title: Area of each small droplet
steps.text: Area scales with diameter squared, so each small droplet has {r}² = {each} times less area than the large one.

steps.title: Total area
steps.text: {n} droplets × (1/{each} of the original area each) = {gain} times the original area.

results.label: Increase in fat surface
results.normal: Dividing the diameter by some number multiplies the surface by that same number.

meaning.text: The fat now offers {gain} times as much surface, so pancreatic lipase has {gain} times as much to work on. Bile salts do no chemical digestion. This physical change is their first job, and you will see a second one, carrying the digested fat to the lining, in Chemical digestion and absorption. Without bile salts, fat is digested more slowly and much of it is lost in the feces.

presets.label: A smaller split: 1 mm to 0.1 mm

asks.prompt: A fat droplet {D} mm across is emulsified into droplets {d} mm across, with the same total volume. By how many times does the total surface grow?

calculators.title: SGLT1: can glucose still enter?
calculators.short: compare the sodium and glucose gradients
calculators.intro: SGLT1 carries two sodium ions and one glucose together, or nothing. Sodium running down its steep gradient can drag glucose up a gentler one. Enter the concentrations on each side of the brush border. The tool compares the two concentration ratios; it does not calculate energies, and the cell’s negative inside adds a further pull on sodium.
calculators.formula: Sodium ratio = [Na+] lumen ÷ [Na+] cell; glucose ratio = [glucose] cell ÷ [glucose] lumen

steps.title: Glucose’s own gradient
steps.text: Glucose is {gi} mM inside and {go} mM in the lumen: a ratio of {gRatio}. Above 1 means the cell already holds more, so glucose alone would diffuse out, and a simple carrier could not absorb it.

steps.title: Sodium’s gradient
steps.text: Sodium is {nao} mM in the lumen and {nai} mM inside: {naRatio} times higher outside. The negative inside of the cell adds to the inward push on this positive ion.

steps.title: Coupling
steps.text: SGLT1 moves two sodium ions with each glucose, or nothing. When two sodium ions have a steep gradient to run down, they release more energy than one glucose uses climbing a gentler one, so the pair moves in.

steps.title: What keeps sodium low inside
steps.text: Sodium–potassium pumps on the basolateral membrane spend ATP to push sodium out. Stop them, and sodium inside rises toward {nao} mM and the ratio falls toward 1: SGLT1 loses its power source.

results.label: Sodium gradient (lumen ÷ cell)
results.normal: About 140 ÷ 15, over 9, while the pumps run.

meaning.text: With sodium only {naRatio} times higher outside, the gradient has collapsed, as when the sodium–potassium pumps stop. SGLT1 has no energy source, so it cannot move glucose against its gradient, even though SGLT1 itself never uses ATP.
Glucose is at least as concentrated in the lumen as in the cell, so it is moving downhill. SGLT1, driven by a sodium gradient of {naRatio}, carries it in easily, as early in a meal.

Glucose would have to climb a ratio of {gRatio}. Even counting the pull of the cell’s negative inside, two sodium ions running down a ratio of {naRatio} cannot supply that much energy, so SGLT1 cannot move glucose in against a gradient this steep.

Glucose has to climb a ratio of {gRatio}, but sodium is {naRatio} times higher outside and two sodium ions move with each glucose. Glucose still enters, powered by the sodium gradient, as late in absorbing a meal.

presets.label: Worked example: late in a meal
Early in a meal: glucose high in the lumen

asks.prompt: Sodium is {nao} mM in the lumen and {nai} mM in the absorptive cell. How many times higher is it outside?
Glucose is {gi} mM in the cell and {go} mM in the lumen. What is the ratio of cell to lumen?

calculators.title: A day’s water balance in the gut
calculators.intro: About 9 L of water pass through your gut each day, and almost all of it comes back. Enter what goes in and what each segment absorbs. The defaults are the chapter figure’s round numbers; gastric juice is usually put at about 2 L a day, and the figure rounds it to 1.5 L.
calculators.formula: Water in feces = (food and drink + secretions) − water absorbed

invalid.when: si > diet + sal + gas + bile + panc + int
invalid.text: The small intestine cannot absorb more than reaches it.

invalid.when: col > diet + sal + gas + bile + panc + int - si + cs
invalid.text: The colon cannot absorb more than reaches it.

derived.expr: diet + sal + gas + bile + panc + int
diet + sal + gas + bile + panc + int + cs
diet + sal + gas + bile + panc + int + cs - si - col
(si + col) / (diet + sal + gas + bile + panc + int + cs) * 100
diet + sal + gas + bile + panc + int - si + cs
si / (diet + sal + gas + bile + panc + int) * 100
col / (diet + sal + gas + bile + panc + int - si + cs) * 100

steps.title: Total water in
steps.text: {diet} + {sal} + {gas} + {bile} + {panc} + {int} = {upper} mL from food, drink and the upper secretions. Add the colon’s {cs} mL: {total} mL in all.

steps.title: Total absorbed
steps.text: {si} + {col} = {absorbed} mL.

steps.title: Left in the feces
steps.text: {total} − {absorbed} = {feces} mL.

steps.title: Percentage absorbed
steps.text: {absorbed} ÷ {total} = {pct}%.

steps.title: Each segment’s share
steps.text: The small intestine absorbed {si} of the {upper} mL that reached it: {siPct}%. The colon absorbed {col} of the {toColon} mL that reached it: {colPct}%.

results.label: Water in the feces
results.normal: About 100 to 200 mL a day.

bands.label: more than normal: loose or watery stools

results.label: Water absorbed
results.normal: About 98%.

meaning.text: {feces} mL of stool water a day is diarrhea on a large scale. The colon can absorb up to about 4 to 5 L a day when more reaches it, so stool water climbs this high only when that reserve is overwhelmed or the colon itself absorbs less. In cholera over 10 L a day can be lost, with sodium, potassium and bicarbonate.

{feces} mL is more than the usual 100 to 200 mL, so stools are looser. Even a small fall in the percentage absorbed shows up as a large change in the stool, because so much water passes through the gut.
Only {feces} mL is left, less than usual: the stools will be hard. More time in the colon, as in constipation, lets it absorb more.
About {feces} mL leaves in the feces, and {pct}% of the water is absorbed. Mass balance: water in = water absorbed + water in the feces.

Small intestine absorbs 1 L less; colon absorbs the same
Small intestine absorbs 1 L less; colon uses its reserve

calculators.title: Energy in a meal
calculators.intro: Enter the grams of each macronutrient in a food or meal. Carbohydrate and protein give about 4 kcal per gram, fat about 9 and alcohol about 7. Vitamins, minerals, water and fiber add almost nothing.
calculators.formula: Energy (kcal) = 4 × carbohydrate (g) + 4 × protein (g) + 9 × fat (g) + 7 × alcohol (g)

invalid.text: Enter at least one macronutrient: with no carbohydrate, protein, fat or alcohol there is no energy to count.

steps.title: Carbohydrate
steps.text: {carb} g × 4 kcal/g = {kc} kcal.

steps.title: Protein
steps.text: {prot} g × 4 kcal/g = {kp} kcal.

steps.title: Fat
steps.text: {fat} g × 9 kcal/g = {kf} kcal.

steps.title: Alcohol
steps.text: {alc} g × 7 kcal/g = {ka} kcal.

steps.title: Add
steps.text: {kc} + {kp} + {kf} + {ka} = {total} kcal (× 4.184 = {kj} kJ).

steps.title: Share from fat
steps.text: {kf} ÷ {total} = {pf}% of the energy, although fat is only {wf}% of the {grams} g by weight. Compare energy, not grams.

results.label: Energy
results.normal: A food label’s "Calories" are kilocalories.

meaning.text: More than half of the {total} kcal come from fat ({pf}%). Each gram of fat carries more than twice the energy of a gram of carbohydrate or protein, because it is mostly carbon–hydrogen bonds with few oxygen atoms.
{ka} of the {total} kcal come from alcohol. Alcohol supplies energy but nothing else the body needs, so it is not a nutrient.
The meal supplies about {total} kcal, {pf}% of it from fat. Vitamins, minerals and water in the food add no energy.

presets.label: Worked example: turkey sandwich (40 g carbohydrate, 25 g protein, 12 g fat)
A sports drink: 35 g of sugar
A handful of peanuts: 6 g carbohydrate, 7 g protein, 14 g fat
A can of beer: 13 g carbohydrate, 2 g protein, 14 g alcohol

calculators.title: Grams from the kilocalories on a label
calculators.intro: Work backward from a label. If all of a food’s energy comes from one macronutrient, dividing the kilocalories by that nutrient’s kcal per gram gives its grams.
calculators.formula: Grams = kilocalories ÷ kcal per gram (4 for carbohydrate or protein, 9 for fat, 7 for alcohol)

inputs.label: Energy per gram of the nutrient

invalid.text: Use 4 (carbohydrate or protein), 7 (alcohol) or 9 (fat).

steps.title: Write the relation
steps.text: kcal = grams × {per} kcal/g.

steps.title: Rearrange
steps.text: grams = kcal ÷ {per}.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.text: {kcal} ÷ {per} = {g} g.

meaning.text: {g} g of carbohydrate (or protein). If it is sugar, that is about {tsp} teaspoons, at about 4 g per teaspoon.
{g} g of fat. The same kilocalories need fewer than half as many grams of fat as of sugar.
{g} g of alcohol.

presets.label: Worked example: a sports drink, 140 kcal all from sugar
A tablespoon of oil: 120 kcal all from fat
A glass of wine: 98 kcal from alcohol
