calculators.title: ATP from one glucose
calculators.short: ATP = 4 direct + NADH × value + FADH2 × value
calculators.intro: Count the ATP made from one glucose broken down fully with oxygen. Current values are about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2. The 2 NADH from glycolysis are made in the cytosol; a shuttle passes their electrons in, worth 2.5 or 1.5 each. Change the values to see where older counts of 36 to 38 come from.
calculators.formula: ATP = 4 (direct) + 8 mitochondrial NADH × (ATP per NADH) + 2 glycolytic NADH × (shuttle value) + 2 FADH2 × (ATP per FADH2)

steps.title: Glycolysis
steps.text: 2 ATP directly + 2 NADH × {s} = {gly} ATP.

steps.title: Pyruvate to acetyl CoA
steps.text: 2 NADH × {n} = {pyr} ATP.

steps.title: Citric acid cycle
steps.text: 2 ATP directly + 6 NADH × {n} ({cn}) + 2 FADH2 × {f} ({cf}) = {cac} ATP.

steps.title: Add
steps.text: {gly} + {pyr} + {cac} = {total} ATP per glucose.

steps.title: Split by method
steps.text: Substrate-level phosphorylation: 4. Oxidative phosphorylation: {ox}, about {oxp}% of the total.

results.label: ATP per glucose
results.normal: About 30 to 32 with current values; 36 to 38 in older counts.

meaning.text: {total} ATP uses whole-number values like the older textbooks. Current measurements of the H+ each carrier’s electrons pump, and the H+ ATP synthase uses (including moving ATP out of the mitochondrion), give about 2.5 and 1.5, and 30 to 32 in all. Give 36–38 if your exam expects it.

{total} ATP per glucose, {oxp}% of them made by oxidative phosphorylation. The 30 to 32 ATP capture a third or more of the 686 kcal per mole released by oxidizing glucose; the rest is released as heat.

presets.label: Older exam values, shuttle to FADH2 (36)

asks.prompt: Count {n} ATP per NADH, {f} per FADH2, and {s} for each NADH made in glycolysis. How many ATP does one glucose yield in all?

calculators.exam: Many textbooks and exams still say 36 or 38 ATP per glucose, from whole-number values of 3 per NADH and 2 per FADH2.

calculators.title: ATP from a fatty acid
calculators.short: ATP = turns × (NADH + FADH2 values) + acetyl CoA × 10 − 2
calculators.intro: A saturated fatty acid with an even number of carbons is cut by beta oxidation into two-carbon acetyl CoA. Each turn makes 1 NADH and 1 FADH2; each acetyl CoA passed through the citric acid cycle yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 ATP (10 ATP at current values). Activation costs the equivalent of 2 ATP once.
calculators.formula: ATP = (C ÷ 2 − 1) × (NADH value + FADH2 value) + (C ÷ 2) × (3 × NADH value + FADH2 value + 1) − 2

invalid.text: Use an even number of carbons: beta oxidation cuts the chain two carbons at a time.

steps.title: Count the turns
steps.text: {C} carbons ÷ 2 = {ac} acetyl CoA, made in {C} ÷ 2 − 1 = {turns} turns (the last turn leaves two acetyl CoA).

steps.title: Carriers from beta oxidation
steps.text: {turns} FADH2 × {f} = {fb}; {turns} NADH × {n} = {nb}. Subtotal {beta} ATP.

steps.title: Acetyl CoA through the cycle
steps.text: Each acetyl CoA yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 ATP: {per} ATP. {ac} × {per} = {cyc} ATP.

steps.title: Subtract the activation cost
steps.text: {beta} + {cyc} − 2 = {total} ATP.

steps.title: Per carbon
steps.text: {total} ÷ {C} = {perC} ATP per carbon, against about 5.3 per carbon for glucose (32 ÷ 6).

results.label: ATP per fatty acid
results.normal: Palmitic acid (16 carbons): about 106.

meaning.text: {total} ATP, about {perC} per carbon. A fatty acid’s carbons are less oxidized to start with than glucose’s, so each has more electrons to hand to the chain. All of it depends on oxygen: there is no anaerobic route for fat.

asks.prompt: A saturated fatty acid has {C} carbons. Using 2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 per FADH2 and 2 ATP to activate it, how many ATP does its complete oxidation yield?

calculators.title: Metabolic rate from oxygen use
calculators.intro: Almost all ATP is made by oxidative phosphorylation, so oxygen use tracks energy use: on a mixed diet, each liter of oxygen consumed releases about 4.8 kcal from fuel. Enter a resting oxygen use to estimate basal metabolic rate.
calculators.formula: Metabolic rate (kcal/day) = O2 use (mL/min) × 1,440 min/day ÷ 1,000 × 4.8 kcal/L

steps.title: Oxygen per day
steps.text: {vo2} mL/min × 60 min/h × 24 h/day = {vo2} × 1,440 = {L} L/day.

steps.title: Energy per liter
steps.text: About {eq} kcal for each liter of oxygen.

steps.title: Multiply
steps.text: {L} L/day × {eq} kcal/L = {day} kcal/day.

steps.title: Per hour
steps.text: {day} ÷ 24 = {hr} kcal/h, about {W} watts of heat.

results.label: Metabolic rate
results.normal: BMR for most adults: about 1,200 to 1,800 kcal a day.

bands.label: below the usual adult BMR range
within the usual adult BMR range
above the usual adult BMR range

{day} kcal/day is above the usual BMR range. A large, muscular body, hyperthyroidism, fever (about 10 to 12% per °C) or recent activity would all raise it.
{day} kcal/day is below the usual adult range, as in a small body, hypothyroidism or a long fast.
About {day} kcal a day, or {hr} kcal an hour, all of it ending as heat. BMR is usually 60 to 70% of total daily energy use.

calculators.title: Energy balance and fat stored or lost
calculators.short: kg of fat ≈ daily balance × days ÷ 7,700
calculators.intro: Adipose tissue holds about 7,700 kcal per kilogram (about 3,500 kcal per pound). Enter a daily surplus (positive) or deficit (negative) and a number of days for a rough first estimate.
calculators.formula: Fat stored or lost (kg) ≈ daily energy balance (kcal/day) × days ÷ 7,700 kcal/kg

invalid.text: With intake equal to spending, the balance is zero and stores do not change.

steps.title: Balance over the whole period
steps.text: {bal} kcal/day × {days} days = {tot} kcal.

steps.title: Convert to fat
steps.text: {tot} ÷ {kpk} kcal/kg = {kg} kg (or {tot} ÷ 3,500 = {lb} lb).

meaning.text: About {kg} kg of fat. The scale will show more in the first week, because glycogen and the water stored with it are lost too.

About {kg} kg by simple division, but over months this overestimates the change: as weight changes, energy spending changes with it, and after weight loss appetite rises too. The real change slows and levels off.
About {kg} kg of fat: a fair first estimate over a few weeks. Weight change slows over time because spending adjusts as weight changes.

presets.label: Worked example: one extra 250 kcal snack a day for 30 days
A 500 kcal daily deficit for one week
A 500 kcal daily deficit for a year

asks.prompt: A person’s daily energy balance is {bal} kcal for {days} days. Using 7,700 kcal per kilogram of adipose tissue, about how many kilograms of fat are stored (+) or lost (−)?

calculators.exam: Many courses use 3,500 kcal per pound and simple division. That is a fair estimate for a few weeks; the first week’s loss is larger, and over months it overestimates the change.

calculators.title: Body mass index
calculators.intro: Body mass index is weight in kilograms divided by the square of height in meters: a quick screen for whether weight is in the range linked to the lowest health risk. It does not measure fat.
calculators.formula: BMI (kg/m²) = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: {kg} ÷ {m2} = {bmi} kg/m².

steps.title: Healthy range for this height
steps.text: 18.5 × {m2} to 24.9 × {m2}: about {lo} to {hi} kg.

results.label: BMI
results.normal: 18.5 to 24.9 for adults.

meaning.text: A BMI of {bmi} is in the obesity range. A very muscular person can score this high with little fat, so BMI is a screen, not a diagnosis; waist size shows fat inside the abdomen, which carries more risk.
A BMI of {bmi} is in the overweight range. People of South Asian and East Asian ancestry develop the linked risks at lower BMIs, so lower cutoffs are often used for them.
A BMI of {bmi} is underweight.
A BMI of {bmi} is in the healthy range. An older adult who has lost muscle can have a normal BMI with a lot of fat.

asks.prompt: An adult weighs {kg} kg and is {m} m tall. What is the BMI?

calculators.title: Sweat needed to shed heat
calculators.intro: In air as warm as the skin, evaporation is the only way left to lose heat. Each liter of sweat that evaporates removes about 580 kcal; sweat that drips off removes almost none. Enter the heat to remove and the share of sweat that evaporates.
calculators.formula: Sweat evaporated (L/h) = heat to remove (kcal/h) ÷ 580 kcal/L; sweat secreted = evaporated ÷ share that evaporates

inputs.label: Share of the sweat that evaporates

steps.title: Heat removed per liter
steps.text: About 580 kcal for each liter that evaporates.

steps.title: Sweat that must be secreted
steps.text: Only {share}% evaporates, so {ev} ÷ {share}% = {sec} L/h; the other {drip} L/h drips off and removes almost no heat.

results.label: Sweat secreted
results.normal: Sweat rates can reach 1 to 2 L an hour, and more after training in the heat.

bands.label: a high but possible sweat rate
more than most people can sweat: heat builds up

meaning.text: {sec} L/h is more than most people can sweat, so heat is stored and core temperature climbs: the setting for exertional heat stroke. Slowing down cuts heat production directly.
Humid air lets only {share}% of the sweat evaporate, so {sec} L/h must be secreted to remove {heat} kcal/h, and all of it is water lost from the body.
{ev} L of sweat must evaporate each hour. That much water and salt is lost from the extracellular fluid and must be replaced by drinking.

presets.label: Worked example: runner, 700 kcal/h, all sweat evaporates
Same runner in humid air: half the sweat evaporates
Walking in hot, dry air: 250 kcal/h

asks.prompt: A cyclist must shed {heat} kcal of heat an hour by sweating, and {share}% of her sweat evaporates. Using 580 kcal per liter evaporated, how many liters of sweat must she secrete each hour?

calculators.title: Net filtration pressure at the glomerulus
calculators.intro: Three pressures decide how hard fluid is pushed out of the glomerular capillaries into the capsule. Enter them to find the net filtration pressure (NFP). The capsular colloid osmotic pressure is left out because the filtrate holds almost no protein. Careful: here CHP is the capsular hydrostatic pressure, the pressure in the capsule, which pushes back. In the capillary exchange calculator, CHP meant capillary hydrostatic pressure; at the glomerulus that pressure is GBHP.
calculators.formula: NFP = GBHP − (CHP + BCOP)

inputs.label: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure (pushes out)
inputs.hint: About 55, held high by the efferent arteriole.

inputs.label: Capsular hydrostatic pressure (pushes back)
inputs.hint: About 15; rises when outflow is blocked. CHP here means the capsule, not the capillary.

inputs.label: Blood colloid osmotic pressure, average (pulls back)

steps.title: The pressure pushing fluid out
steps.text: Only GBHP pushes fluid out of the glomerulus: {GBHP} mm Hg.

steps.title: The pressures pushing fluid back
steps.text: CHP pushes back from the capsule and BCOP pulls back into the blood: {CHP} + {BCOP} = {back} mm Hg.

steps.title: Subtract
steps.text: NFP = {GBHP} − {back} = {NFP:+} mm Hg.

steps.title: Read the sign and size
steps.text: A positive NFP means fluid is filtered into the capsule; zero or below means no filtration. Compared with a normal NFP of about 10 mm Hg, this is a change of {change:+}%. Because the pushing and pulling pressures nearly balance, a small change in any one of them changes NFP, and so filtration, a lot.

results.label: Net filtration pressure
results.normal: About +10 mm Hg.

meaning.text: With an NFP of {NFP:+} mm Hg, the pressures pushing back match or beat GBHP, so filtration stops. The glomerulus does not take fluid back in; it simply stops filtering.
An NFP of {NFP:+} mm Hg is below the normal 10, so with the same filtration coefficient, GFR falls by about the same share.
An NFP of {NFP:+} mm Hg is above normal, so filtration rises. In a real kidney, autoregulation pushes back, so GFR rises less than this suggests.
An NFP of {NFP:+} mm Hg is about normal. That small push drives about 180 liters of filtrate a day.
CHP is raised, as when a ureter or the urethra is blocked and filtrate backs up into the capsule.
BCOP is low, as when plasma albumin is low, so less pull holds fluid in the capillaries.
GBHP is low, as when the afferent arterioles constrict or arterial pressure falls below the autoregulatory range.

presets.label: Worked example 2: GBHP falls after a bleed

asks.prompt: At the glomerulus, GBHP = {GBHP} mm Hg, CHP = {CHP} mm Hg and the average BCOP = {BCOP} mm Hg. What is the net filtration pressure?

calculators.title: GFR from Kf and net filtration pressure
calculators.intro: GFR depends on how hard fluid is pushed (the net filtration pressure) and how easily it crosses the filter (the filtration coefficient, Kf, set by the filtering area and its permeability). Enter both for the two kidneys together.
calculators.formula: GFR = Kf × NFP

inputs.label: Filtration coefficient, both kidneys
inputs.hint: About 12.5; lower when glomeruli are scarred or mesangial cells contract.

steps.title: Write the equation
steps.text: GFR = Kf × NFP.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.text: GFR = {Kf} mL/min per mm Hg × {NFP} mm Hg. The mm Hg units cancel.

steps.title: Calculate
steps.text: GFR = {GFR} mL/min, {pct}% of a normal 125 mL/min.

steps.title: Per day
steps.text: A day has 60 × 24 = 1,440 minutes: {GFR} mL/min × 1,440 min ÷ 1,000 = about {perDay} L of filtrate a day.

results.label: Glomerular filtration rate
results.normal: About 125 mL/min in a healthy young adult, about 10% lower in women.

results.label: Filtrate per day
results.normal: About 180 L a day.

meaning.text: A GFR of {GFR} mL/min means less plasma is cleared of wastes each minute, so urea and other wastes start to build up in the blood if it lasts.
A GFR of {GFR} mL/min pushes fluid through the tubules faster than normal, so they have less time to reabsorb salt, water and nutrients.
A GFR of {GFR} mL/min, about {perDay} L a day. The tubules must return more than 99% of it.
Kf is low, as when glomeruli are scarred or lost with age. GFR can fall even when every pressure is normal.

asks.prompt: Both kidneys have a filtration coefficient of {Kf} mL/min per mm Hg, and the net filtration pressure is {NFP} mm Hg. What is the GFR?

calculators.title: Filtration fraction
calculators.intro: Only part of the plasma reaching the glomeruli is filtered; the rest leaves in the efferent arterioles. Enter renal blood flow, hematocrit and GFR to find what share is filtered.
calculators.formula: Renal plasma flow = renal blood flow × (1 − hematocrit); FF = GFR ÷ renal plasma flow

invalid.text: GFR cannot be as large as the plasma flow reaching the glomeruli.

steps.title: Find the plasma share of blood
steps.text: Plasma is the part that is not cells: 100 − {Hct} = {plasmaPct}%.

steps.title: Renal plasma flow
steps.text: {RBF} mL/min × {plasmaPct}% = {RPF} mL/min of plasma reaches the glomeruli.

steps.title: Divide GFR by plasma flow
steps.text: FF = {GFR} ÷ {RPF} = {FF}%.

steps.title: What leaves
steps.text: {RPF} − {GFR} = {left} mL/min of plasma leaves in the efferent arterioles, richer in protein, and flows on to the peritubular capillaries.

results.label: Filtration fraction
results.normal: About 20%.

meaning.text: A filtration fraction of {FF}% means more of each milliliter of plasma is filtered, as when the efferent arterioles constrict. The blood leaving the glomerulus is especially rich in protein, which pulls reabsorbed fluid into the peritubular capillaries.
A filtration fraction of {FF}% means relatively little of the plasma is filtered, as when blood flow is high but glomerular pressure is not.
About {FF}% of the plasma reaching the glomeruli becomes filtrate: roughly one fifth. The other four fifths leave in the efferent arterioles.

asks.prompt: Renal blood flow is {RBF} mL/min, hematocrit is {Hct}% and GFR is {GFR} mL/min. What percentage of the plasma reaching the glomeruli is filtered?

calculators.title: Filtered load and the transport maximum
calculators.short: excreted = filtered load − reabsorbed (capped at Tm)
calculators.intro: How much glucose reaches the tubules each minute, how much the carriers can take back, and how much spills into the urine. Enter GFR, plasma glucose and the transport maximum (Tm).
calculators.formula: Filtered load = GFR × plasma concentration; reabsorbed = the smaller of the load and Tm; excreted = load − reabsorbed

steps.title: Convert the concentration
steps.text: {Pg} mg/dL = {Pg} mg per 100 mL = {conc} mg/mL.

steps.title: Filtered load
steps.text: GFR × concentration = {GFR} mL/min × {conc} mg/mL = {load} mg/min.

steps.title: Compare with Tm
steps.text: The carriers can take back at most {Tm} mg/min, so reabsorbed = {reab} mg/min.

steps.title: Excreted
steps.text: Excreted = filtered − reabsorbed = {load} − {reab} = {excr} mg/min, about {perDay} g a day if it lasted.

results.label: Glucose excreted
results.normal: Zero at a normal plasma glucose.

results.label: Filtered load
results.normal: About 125 mg/min at 100 mg/dL.

meaning.text: The filtered load of {load} mg/min exceeds the carriers’ ceiling, so {excr} mg/min spills into the urine. The glucose left in the tubule holds water with it, which is why untreated diabetes mellitus causes polyuria and thirst.

In this idealized calculation the filtered load of {load} mg/min is still under Tm, so no glucose is excreted. A real kidney would already spill some at {Pg} mg/dL, because that is above the renal threshold of about 180 mg/dL: some nephrons saturate early (the splay).
The filtered load of {load} mg/min is within what the carriers can handle, so all of it is reabsorbed and none is excreted.

calculators.note: This calculation treats every nephron alike, so glucose spills only once the whole load passes Tm (about 300 mg/dL at a GFR of 125). Real kidneys start to spill at about 180 mg/dL, the renal threshold, because some nephrons saturate early (the splay).

asks.prompt: GFR is {GFR} mL/min, plasma glucose is {Pg} mg/dL and the transport maximum is {Tm} mg/min. Treating every nephron alike, how much glucose is excreted each minute?

calculators.title: Filtered load and percentage reabsorbed
calculators.intro: For a substance that is filtered freely and then reabsorbed, find how much is filtered each day, how much comes back and what percentage that is. The defaults are sodium.
calculators.formula: Filtered load = GFR × plasma concentration; reabsorbed = filtered − excreted

inputs.label: Amount excreted in the urine
inputs.hint: Sodium about 100 to 250 mmol a day, matching intake.

invalid.text: More is excreted than is filtered, so the tubule must be secreting it; this calculator is for substances with net reabsorption.

steps.title: Filtered load
steps.text: GFR × plasma concentration = {GFR} L/day × {P} mmol/L = {load} mmol/day.

steps.title: Reabsorbed
steps.text: Filtered − excreted = {load} − {E} = {reab} mmol/day.

steps.title: Percentage
steps.text: {reab} ÷ {load} × 100 = {pct}%.

steps.title: Why small changes matter
steps.text: A change of just 1% in reabsorption changes excretion by {onePct} mmol a day.

results.label: Percentage reabsorbed
results.normal: About 99.4% for sodium.

results.label: Filtered load
results.normal: About 25,000 mmol of sodium a day.

meaning.text: The tubule returns {pct}% of what is filtered. A shift of 1% in reabsorption would move {onePct} mmol a day, which is why the tubule, not the glomerulus, fine-tunes what you excrete.
The tubule returns {pct}% of what is filtered, and the rest, {E} mmol a day, leaves in the urine. Amount excreted = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted.

asks.prompt: GFR is {GFR} L a day and plasma sodium is {P} mmol/L. The urine contains {E} mmol of sodium a day. What percentage of the filtered sodium is reabsorbed?

calculators.title: Obligatory and facultative water reabsorption
calculators.short: water to the collecting duct = filtered × (1 − obligatory share)
calculators.intro: Most filtered water comes back whatever you drink. Enter the water filtered, the share reabsorbed obligatorily, and the urine volume, to see how much water ADH had to work with and how much of it was kept.
calculators.formula: Water reaching the distal parts = filtered − obligatory; facultative = that water − urine

inputs.label: Share reabsorbed obligatorily
inputs.hint: About 80 to 85%; some textbooks round to 90%.

invalid.text: The urine cannot hold more water than reaches the distal tubule and collecting duct.

steps.title: Obligatory reabsorption
steps.text: {ob}% × {F} L = {obL} L comes back in the proximal tubule and descending limb, whatever ADH does.

steps.title: Water left for ADH to work on
steps.text: {F} − {obL} = {distal} L a day reaches the distal tubule and collecting duct.

steps.title: Facultative reabsorption
steps.text: {distal} − {V} = {fac} L was reabsorbed there under ADH: {facPct}% of what reached it.

steps.title: Overall
steps.text: ({F} − {V}) ÷ {F} = {total}% of the filtered water returned to the blood.

results.label: Facultative water reabsorbed
results.normal: About 30 L a day with normal ADH.

results.label: Share of filtered water reabsorbed
results.normal: About 99%.

meaning.text: A urine volume of {V} L a day means the collecting ducts are reabsorbing little of the water that reaches them, as when ADH is missing or the principal cells cannot respond to it (diabetes insipidus).
Only {V} L of urine means ADH is high and the collecting ducts are keeping almost all of the {distal} L that reaches them.
Of {distal} L reaching the collecting ducts, {fac} L was kept. ADH sets this facultative share, and with it the volume of your urine.

calculators.exam: Some textbooks round the split to about 90% obligatory and 10% facultative. The exact figure matters less than the idea: most water returns whatever you drink, and a smaller, adjustable share sets your urine volume.

presets.label: 180 L filtered, 1.5 L of urine (numbers of worked examples 1 and 5)

asks.prompt: A person filters {F} L of water a day, {ob}% of it is reabsorbed obligatorily, and they pass {V} L of urine. How many liters a day are reabsorbed facultatively?

calculators.title: Urine volume from solute load and concentration
calculators.intro: Every day you must excrete about 600 mOsm of waste solute. Enter the solute load and the urine osmolarity to find the volume of urine that carries it, and the least volume possible at the kidney’s maximum of 1,200 mOsm/L.
calculators.formula: Volume = solute ÷ concentration

steps.title: Write the relationship
steps.text: Volume = amount of solute ÷ concentration.

steps.title: This urine
steps.text: {S} mOsm ÷ {U} mOsm/L = {Vol} L a day.

steps.title: The least possible
steps.text: At the maximum of 1,200 mOsm/L: {S} ÷ 1,200 = {Vmin} L a day. Less than that, and waste solute builds up in the blood whatever ADH does.

steps.title: The most dilute
steps.text: At about 50 mOsm/L: {S} ÷ 50 = {Vmax} L a day.

results.label: Urine volume
results.normal: Usually 1 to 2 L a day.

results.label: Least possible volume
results.normal: About 0.5 L for 600 mOsm.

meaning.text: This is the most concentrated urine the kidney can make, so {Vol} L is the least urine that can carry {S} mOsm. On a day without water, the kidneys cannot go below it; only drinking restores the water lost.
Urine at {U} mOsm/L is more dilute than plasma: ADH is low, and the kidney is getting rid of extra water.
At {U} mOsm/L, {S} mOsm needs {Vol} L of urine a day.

asks.prompt: A person must excrete {S} mOsm of solute a day, and their urine is at {U} mOsm/L. What daily urine volume carries it?

calculators.title: Renal clearance
calculators.intro: Renal clearance is the volume of plasma the kidneys completely clear of a substance each minute. Enter its urine and plasma concentrations (in the same units) and the urine flow, then compare the clearance with GFR to see what the tubule does with it.
calculators.formula: C = (U × V) ÷ P

inputs.label: Urine flow
inputs.hint: About 1 mL/min; a 24-hour volume in mL ÷ 1,440.

steps.title: Amount excreted each minute
steps.text: U × V = {U} mg/mL × {V} mL/min = {excr} mg/min.

steps.title: Turn that amount into a volume of plasma
steps.text: Divide by the plasma concentration: {excr} mg/min ÷ {P} mg/mL = {C} mL/min. The mg cancel, leaving mL/min.

steps.title: Compare with GFR
steps.text: Clearance ÷ GFR = {C} ÷ {GFR} = {ratio}.

steps.title: Read the comparison
steps.text: Equal to GFR: filtered only. Below GFR: net reabsorption. Above GFR: net secretion, because the tubule removes the substance from plasma that was never filtered.

results.label: Renal clearance
results.normal: Inulin: equal to GFR. Creatinine: 10 to 20% above GFR. Urea: about 60 to 70 mL/min. Glucose: 0.

meaning.text: A clearance of {C} mL/min is below the GFR of {GFR}, so some of the filtered substance must have been reabsorbed, as with urea (about half reabsorbed) or glucose (all of it).

A clearance of {C} mL/min is close to the GFR of {GFR}. A substance that is filtered freely and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, like inulin, has a clearance equal to GFR, which is how GFR is measured. Creatinine runs 10 to 20% higher because a little is secreted.
A clearance of {C} mL/min is {ratio} times the GFR, more than filtration alone can remove, so the tubule secretes it, like penicillin. Such drugs must be given often to keep blood levels up.

asks.prompt: A substance’s urine concentration is {U} mg/mL, its plasma concentration is {P} mg/mL and urine flow is {V} mL/min. What is its renal clearance?

calculators.title: Plasma creatinine and GFR at steady state
calculators.intro: Muscle makes creatinine at a steady rate, and once things settle, the kidneys excrete it at the same rate, mainly by filtration. Enter the production rate and GFR to find the plasma creatinine they settle at.
calculators.formula: At steady state: production = GFR × plasma creatinine, so plasma creatinine = production ÷ GFR

inputs.label: Creatinine made by muscle
inputs.hint: About 1 to 1.5 mg/min; more with more muscle.

steps.title: Set excretion equal to production
steps.text: At steady state, excretion = production, and excretion ≈ GFR × P. So P = production ÷ GFR.

steps.title: Divide
steps.text: P = {prod} mg/min ÷ {GFR} mL/min = {PmL} mg/mL.

steps.title: Convert to mg/dL
steps.text: 1 dL = 100 mL, so P = {PmL} × 100 = {Pdl} mg/dL.

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: At a GFR of {GFR} mL/min, plasma creatinine settles at {ratio} times the value the same muscle mass gives at a GFR of 120 mL/min: the two move in opposite directions.

results.label: Plasma creatinine
results.normal: About 0.6 to 1.2 mg/dL, depending on muscle mass.

meaning.text: A plasma creatinine of {Pdl} mg/dL means GFR has fallen. Because the link is inverse, halving GFR only doubles creatinine, so early losses can hide behind a value that still looks small. Labs report an estimated GFR from creatinine, age and sex for that reason.
A plasma creatinine of {Pdl} mg/dL is in the usual range for this muscle mass. Note that a GFR loss of up to half can still leave creatinine near the top of that range.

asks.prompt: A man makes {prod} mg of creatinine a minute, and his GFR is steady at {GFR} mL/min. What is his plasma creatinine in mg/dL once it has settled?

calculators.title: Body fluid compartment volumes
calculators.short: TBW → ICF, ECF, interstitial fluid, plasma
calculators.intro: Estimate how much water a person carries and how it splits between the compartments. Total body water is a share of body mass (about 60% in a young man, 50 to 55% in a woman, 45 to 50% in an older adult, 75% in an infant). In an adult, two thirds of it is ICF and one third ECF; the ECF is three quarters interstitial fluid and one quarter plasma.
calculators.formula: TBW = mass × share; ICF = ⅔ TBW; ECF = ⅓ TBW; interstitial = ¾ ECF; plasma = ¼ ECF

inputs.label: Total body water as a share of mass
inputs.hint: About 60% young man, 50–55% woman, 45–50% older adult, 75% infant.

steps.title: Total body water
steps.text: {S}% of {M} kg = {TBW} L (1 kg of water is about 1 L).

steps.title: Intracellular fluid
steps.text: Two thirds of {TBW} L = {ICF} L, inside all your cells.

steps.title: Extracellular fluid
steps.text: One third of {TBW} L = {ECF} L. Check: {ICF} + {ECF} = {TBW} L.

steps.title: Interstitial fluid
steps.text: Three quarters of the ECF: ¾ × {ECF} L = {ISF} L, bathing the cells.

steps.title: Plasma
steps.text: One quarter of the ECF: ¼ × {ECF} L = {PL} L, about one twelfth of all body water.

results.label: Total body water
results.normal: About 42 L in a 70 kg young man (the 60–40–20 rule).

results.label: Plasma
results.normal: About 3 L in an adult.

meaning.text: A share of {S}% is typical of an infant. More of an infant’s weight is water, and they turn over a larger share of it each day, so a day of vomiting or diarrhea is a bigger loss for them. The two-thirds / one-third split is an adult rule: in a newborn the ECF is close to half of body water or more, so these compartment numbers are only rough.
A share of {S}% is typical of a woman or an older adult, who carry more fat or less muscle for their weight. A smaller reserve means the same loss of water is a larger fraction of what they have.

Of {TBW} L of body water, only {PL} L is plasma. Fluid lost from or added to the plasma is soon shared with the much larger interstitial fluid, and water that crosses plasma membranes is shared with the ICF too.

asks.prompt: A {M} kg adult has total body water equal to {S}% of body mass. Estimate the intracellular fluid volume.
A {M} kg adult has total body water equal to {S}% of body mass. Estimate the extracellular fluid volume.
A {M} kg adult has total body water equal to {S}% of body mass. Estimate the plasma volume.

calculators.title: Drinking water fast: the new osmolality
calculators.short: New osmolality = total solute ÷ new body water
calculators.intro: Plain water adds no solute, so drinking it quickly (before the kidneys excrete any) dilutes all your body water at once. Enter body water, starting osmolality and the volume drunk to see the new osmolality and where the water goes.
calculators.formula: Solute = osmolality × water; new osmolality = solute ÷ (water + volume drunk)

steps.title: Total solute
steps.text: Osmolality × water = {O} mOsm/kg × {W} kg = {SOL} mOsm. Water adds none, so this stays the same.

steps.title: New osmolality
steps.text: {SOL} ÷ {W2} = {O2} mOsm/kg, a fall of {DROP}%.

steps.title: Where the water goes
steps.text: Pure water crosses plasma membranes freely and spreads in proportion to compartment size: two thirds, {INC} L, into cells, and one third, {INE} L, in the ECF.

steps.title: How much stays in the plasma
steps.text: One quarter of the ECF share: {INE} ÷ 4 ≈ {INP} mL.

results.label: New plasma osmolality
results.normal: Normal range about 275 to 295; set point about 285 to 290.

results.label: Water that stays in the plasma

meaning.text: A fall of {DROP}% is more than the 1 to 2% the osmoreceptors detect, so ADH release falls, the collecting ducts become nearly waterproof, and the kidneys pass the extra water as dilute urine over the next hours. Most of it, {INC} L, sits inside cells until then, which slightly swells them.
A fall of {DROP}% is at or below what the osmoreceptors detect, so ADH barely changes; the extra water is excreted gradually.

Healthy kidneys excrete a little under 1 L of water an hour. Drinking {D} L faster than that leaves water in cells for hours, and swelling brain cells cause headache, nausea and confusion: water intoxication.

asks.prompt: A person has {W} L of body water at {O} mOsm/kg and drinks {D} L of plain water quickly, before the kidneys excrete any. Estimate the new plasma osmolality.
A person drinks {D} L of plain water quickly. About how many milliliters of it stay in the plasma once it has spread through body water?

calculators.title: A day’s water balance
calculators.intro: Add up a day’s water intake and output. Only two routes are adjusted to keep water in balance, drinking (thirst) and urine (ADH); the others change with fever, heat, breathing and diet.
calculators.formula: Net = (drinks + food + metabolic water) − (urine + insensible loss + sweat + feces)

inputs.label: Insensible loss (skin and breath)
inputs.hint: Rises with fever, fast breathing, dry air and burns.

derived.expr: DR + FO + ME - (UR + IN + SW + FE)
(DR + FO + ME - (UR + IN + SW + FE)) * DAYS
abs(DR + FO + ME - (UR + IN + SW + FE))

steps.title: Intake
steps.text: {DR} + {FO} + {ME} = {IN_T} L/day.

steps.title: Output
steps.text: {UR} + {IN} + {SW} + {FE} = {OUT_T} L/day.

steps.title: Net change per day
steps.text: {IN_T} − {OUT_T} = {NET:+} L/day.

steps.title: Over the whole period
steps.text: {DAYS} × {NET:+} = {TOT:+} L, if nothing else changed.

results.label: Net water change per day
results.normal: Zero: a typical adult takes in and loses about 2.5 L a day.

meaning.text: Output exceeds intake by {NETA} L a day. In practice this is rarely left to run: the rising plasma osmolality raises ADH, which cuts urine output, and switches on thirst, which raises intake. Urine has a floor of about 0.5 L a day, though, so with no water intake at all you lose water every day whatever the kidneys do.
Intake matches output: water balance. Most routes are not adjusted for water; drinking and urine volume are the two that are.
Intake exceeds output by {NETA} L a day. The falling osmolality lowers ADH, so the kidneys pass the extra as dilute urine; healthy kidneys can excrete roughly 0.7 to 1 L an hour.

presets.label: Worked example 2: fever for three days

asks.prompt: Over {DAYS} days a person drinks {DR} L a day, gets {FO} L from food and {ME} L of metabolic water, and loses {UR} L of urine, {IN} L of insensible water, {SW} L of sweat and {FE} L in feces each day. What is the total change in body water (+ for gain, − for loss)?

calculators.title: Estimating plasma osmolality
calculators.intro: Sodium and the anions that travel with it are almost all the solute in the ECF, so a routine blood panel can estimate plasma osmolality. Glucose and urea nitrogen are reported in mg/dL in the United States; dividing converts them to mmol/L.
calculators.formula: Posm ≈ 2 × Na + glucose ÷ 18 + urea nitrogen ÷ 2.8

steps.title: Sodium and its anions
steps.text: Each sodium ion is matched by an anion, mainly chloride or bicarbonate, so count sodium twice: 2 × {NA} = {NA2}.

steps.title: Glucose
steps.text: Dividing by 18 converts mg/dL to mmol/L: {GL} ÷ 18 = {GM}.

steps.title: Add
steps.text: {NA2} + {GM} + {UM} = {OSM} mOsm/kg.

results.label: Estimated plasma osmolality
results.normal: About 275 to 295.

meaning.text: An osmolality of {OSM} mOsm/kg is high. If it comes from sodium or, without insulin, from glucose, water leaves cells and they shrink.
An osmolality of {OSM} mOsm/kg is low, usually because there is too much water for the sodium. Water enters cells, and swelling brain cells cause the symptoms.
An osmolality of {OSM} mOsm/kg is in the normal range. Sodium and its anions supply {NA2} of it.

Glucose at {GL} mg/dL adds {GM} mmol/L. Without insulin it stays outside most cells and draws water out of them, and that water dilutes the plasma sodium: very high glucose lowers the measured sodium.
Urea at {BU} mg/dL adds {UM}, but urea crosses cell membranes, so it raises the measured osmolality without drawing water out of cells. Only solutes that stay outside cells set tonicity.

asks.prompt: Sodium {NA} mmol/L, glucose {GL} mg/dL, urea nitrogen {BU} mg/dL. Estimate the plasma osmolality.

calculators.title: Why small potassium shifts matter
calculators.short: Rise = cell K+ moved ÷ ECF volume
calculators.intro: About 98% of body potassium is inside cells and the ECF holds only about 60 mmol. Enter the share of cell potassium that moves out (positive, as in a crush injury) or in (negative, as after insulin) and see what happens to plasma potassium before the kidneys act.
calculators.formula: New K+ = starting K+ + (cell K+ × share moved) ÷ ECF volume

inputs.label: Share of cell potassium moved out (− for into cells)

invalid.text: That would move more potassium into cells than the ECF holds. Try a smaller share.

steps.title: Potassium moved
steps.text: {F:+}% of {KC} mmol = {MOV:+} mmol.

steps.title: Change in concentration
steps.text: Spread through {V} L of ECF: {MOV:+} ÷ {V} = {DK:+} mmol/L.

results.label: New plasma potassium
results.normal: About 3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L.

meaning.text: Shifting potassium into cells changed plasma potassium by {DK:+} mmol/L, to {K1} mmol/L, which is still high. A shift into cells buys time, but it leaves the body’s total potassium unchanged; the extra potassium must still be removed by the kidneys, binders or dialysis.

A plasma potassium of {K1} mmol/L is dangerous: moving just {F}% of cell potassium did it. The resting potential of heart cells moves toward threshold, with peaked T waves and a risk of ventricular fibrillation. IV calcium protects the heart while insulin shifts potassium back into cells.
A plasma potassium of {K1} mmol/L is high. Because the ECF holds so little potassium, a small shift out of cells shows up fast.
A plasma potassium of {K1} mmol/L is low. The same small ECF that makes shifts out dangerous makes shifts in, as with insulin treatment, lower the plasma value quickly.
A plasma potassium of {K1} mmol/L is in range. The shift changed it by {DK:+} mmol/L without changing the body’s total potassium.

asks.prompt: Cells hold {KC} mmol of potassium and the ECF is {V} L at {K0} mmol/L. If {F}% of the cell potassium moves out of cells (a negative share means into cells), what is the new plasma potassium, before any is excreted?

calculators.title: Converting mg/dL to mmol/L and mEq/L
calculators.short: mmol/L = mg/dL × 10 ÷ atomic mass; mEq = mmol × charge
calculators.intro: Labs report electrolytes in three units: mmol/L counts particles, mEq/L counts charge, and mg/dL is a mass, used in the United States for calcium, phosphate and magnesium. Convert one to the others.
calculators.formula: mmol/L = (mg/dL × 10) ÷ atomic mass; mEq/L = mmol/L × charge

steps.title: Convert to mg/L
steps.text: A deciliter is 0.1 L, so {C} mg/dL = {MGL} mg/L.

steps.title: Convert to mmol/L
steps.text: One millimole weighs {A} mg: {MGL} ÷ {A} = {MM} mmol/L.

steps.title: Convert to mEq/L
steps.text: Each ion carries {Z} charges: {MM} × {Z} = {ME} mEq/L.

results.label: Concentration
results.normal: Total calcium about 2.1 to 2.6 mmol/L (8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL).

meaning.text: For an ion with one charge, such as sodium, potassium or chloride, mmol/L and mEq/L are the same number.
{C} mg/dL is {MM} mmol/L. Because each ion carries {Z} charges, that is {ME} mEq/L of charge.

presets.label: Calcium at the lower limit, 8.5 mg/dL

asks.prompt: A total calcium is {C} mg/dL. Calcium’s atomic mass is 40. Express it in mmol/L.
A total calcium is {C} mg/dL. Calcium’s atomic mass is 40 and it carries two charges. Express it in mEq/L.

calculators.title: Calcium adjusted for a low albumin
calculators.intro: About 40% of plasma calcium rides on proteins, mainly albumin. When albumin is low, total calcium reads low even if the ionized calcium, the part that acts on cells, is normal. This bedside estimate adds back the calcium the missing albumin would have carried.
calculators.formula: Adjusted calcium = measured calcium + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin)

steps.title: Calcium that shortfall would have bound
steps.text: 0.8 × {SH} = {ADD} mg/dL.

steps.title: Adjusted calcium
steps.text: {CA} + {ADD} = {ADJ} mg/dL.

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: The usual range for total calcium is 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL.

results.label: Adjusted calcium (estimate)
results.normal: 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL.

meaning.text: The measured {CA} mg/dL looks low, but the adjusted value of {ADJ} mg/dL is in range, which suggests the low total may just reflect the low albumin.
Even adjusted, the calcium is low ({ADJ} mg/dL), which points to a real hypocalcemia.
The adjusted calcium, {ADJ} mg/dL, is high: a low albumin can hide a hypercalcemia.
The adjusted calcium is {ADJ} mg/dL, within the usual range.

calculators.note: This is only an estimate. It misclassifies patients most often in exactly the setting it is used for, a very low albumin, and can hide a real hypocalcemia. When the answer matters, the lab measures ionized calcium directly.

asks.prompt: A patient’s total calcium is {CA} mg/dL and albumin {AL} g/dL. Using adjusted calcium = measured + 0.8 × (4.0 − albumin), estimate the adjusted calcium.

calculators.title: How fast is the sodium being corrected?
calculators.intro: Brain cells adapt to a long-standing low or high sodium over about two days, so a chronic disorder must be corrected slowly: a low sodium raised by no more than about 8 to 10 mmol/L in the first 24 hours, and a high sodium lowered by no more than about 10 mmol/L a day. Enter the change so far to see the pace.
calculators.formula: Rate = (sodium now − starting sodium) × 24 ÷ hours elapsed

inputs.label: Change so far (− for a fall)

steps.title: Scale to 24 hours
steps.text: {DN:+} mmol/L in {H} h × (24 ÷ {H}) = {R:+} mmol/L per 24 h, if the same pace continues.

steps.title: Compare with the limit
steps.text: Chronic low sodium: no more than about 8 to 10 mmol/L up in the first 24 hours. Chronic high sodium: no more than about 10 mmol/L down per day.

bands.label: too fast for a chronic disorder

meaning.text: Raising a chronic low sodium by {R} mmol/L per 24 hours is too fast. Brain cells that have shed potassium and organic solutes lose water to the more concentrated ECF and shrink, and the myelin of the pons can be damaged (osmotic demyelination), with paralysis and trouble speaking and swallowing days later.

Lowering a chronic high sodium by {AR} mmol/L per 24 hours is faster than the usual advice. Brain cells that have gained solute can take in water and swell, a danger shown mainly in infants and children.
A pace of {R:+} mmol/L per 24 hours is at the edge of the usual limits; the sodium would be rechecked often and the treatment slowed if needed.
A pace of {R:+} mmol/L per 24 hours is within the usual limit for a chronic disorder, so adapted brain cells have time to regain or shed solute.
The limit applies to chronic low sodium. Sudden, severe low sodium with seizures is different: the brain has not adapted, and small doses of 3% saline are given quickly.

presets.label: Chronic low sodium: a safe pace

asks.prompt: A patient with chronic low sodium starts at {N0} mmol/L. After {H} hours of treatment it has risen by {DN} mmol/L. At that pace, how much would it rise in 24 hours?

calculators.title: Blood pH from bicarbonate and PCO2
calculators.intro: Blood pH depends on the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide, not on either amount alone. The kidneys set the top of the ratio and the lungs the bottom. Normally the ratio is 20 to 1 and pH is 7.40.

steps.title: Dissolved carbon dioxide
steps.text: Each mm Hg dissolves 0.03 mmol/L: 0.03 × {P} = {D} mmol/L.

steps.title: The ratio
steps.text: {H} ÷ {D} = {R} (normally 20).

steps.title: The log
steps.text: log {R} = {LG}. Without a calculator: log 10 = 1.0, log 12.5 = 1.1, log 16 = 1.2, log 20 = 1.3, log 25 = 1.4, log 32 = 1.5.

results.label: HCO3− : dissolved CO2
results.normal: About 20 to 1.

meaning.text: The ratio of {R} is below 20, so the pH, {PH}, is below the normal range. Halving the ratio lowers pH by 0.3; either less bicarbonate or more carbon dioxide can do it.
The ratio of {R} is above 20, so the pH, {PH}, is above the normal range. Doubling the ratio raises pH by 0.3.
A ratio of {R} gives a pH of {PH}, in range. Notice that the same pH can come from very different amounts, as long as the ratio stays near 20.

presets.label: Worked example 3: acid uses half the bicarbonate
Worked example 5: too much carbon dioxide

asks.prompt: Arterial bicarbonate is {H} mmol/L and PCO2 is {P} mm Hg. What is the pH?
Arterial bicarbonate is {H} mmol/L and PCO2 is {P} mm Hg. What is the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide?

calculators.title: Net acid excretion
calculators.short: NAE = titratable acid + ammonium − bicarbonate lost
calculators.intro: Acid–base balance is mass balance: over a day, the acid the kidneys excrete must equal the fixed acid you make. Enter a 24-hour urine and the day’s fixed acid production.
calculators.formula: Net acid excretion = titratable acid + ammonium − bicarbonate in urine

steps.title: Add the acid excreted
steps.text: {TA} + {NH} = {AC} mmol.

steps.title: Subtract the base lost
steps.text: Each bicarbonate lost cancels one H+ excreted: {AC} − {B} = {NAE} mmol/day.

steps.title: Compare with production
steps.text: {NAE} excreted − {F} made = {DIF:+} mmol/day.

results.label: Net acid excretion
results.normal: About 50 to 100 mmol/day on a mixed diet, matching production.

meaning.text: The kidneys excrete {NAE} mmol but {F} mmol is made, so about {DEF} mmol of acid a day stays in the body, using up bicarbonate. This is what happens between dialysis sessions in kidney failure: plasma bicarbonate drifts down day after day.
Net acid excretion ({NAE} mmol/day) matches production ({F} mmol/day) within measurement error, so plasma bicarbonate stays steady.
The kidneys are excreting {DIF} mmol a day more than is being made, adding new bicarbonate: what happens while they rebuild bicarbonate after an acid load.

Ammonium at {NH} mmol/day is well above its usual 30 to 50. Ammonium is the adjustable route: over 3 to 5 days of acid load it can rise five- to tenfold, while titratable acid is limited by filtered phosphate.

presets.label: Five days into a large acid load

asks.prompt: In 24 hours a person excretes {TA} mmol of titratable acid, {NH} mmol of ammonium and {B} mmol of bicarbonate. What is the net acid excretion?

calculators.title: Why urine needs buffers
calculators.short: Volume = acid ÷ free H+ per liter
calculators.intro: Proton pumps cannot drive urine pH below about 4.5, and at that pH very few hydrogen ions are free. Work out how much urine it would take to excrete the day’s fixed acid as free H+ alone.
calculators.formula: [H+] = 10^−pH mol/L; volume = acid ÷ [H+]

steps.title: Free H+ per liter
steps.text: [H+] = 10^−{PH} mol/L = {HM} mmol/L.

steps.title: Volume needed
steps.text: {A} mmol ÷ {HM} mmol/L = {VOL} L of urine.

results.label: Urine needed to carry the acid as free H+
results.normal: Actual urine: about 1.5 L a day.

meaning.text: Excreting {A} mmol of acid as free H+ at pH {PH} would take about {VOL} L of urine. In reality well under 0.1 mmol a day leaves as free H+. The rest is carried on phosphate (titratable acid, about 20 to 30 mmol a day) and ammonia (ammonium, about 30 to 50 mmol a day, and adjustable).

asks.prompt: Urine pH is {PH}. How many liters of urine would it take to excrete {A} mmol of acid as free H+ alone?

calculators.title: Stepwise arterial blood gas interpreter
calculators.short: pH, then PaCO2, then HCO3−, then compensation
calculators.intro: The three acid–base numbers of an ABG are tied together: pH = 6.1 + log(HCO3− ÷ (0.03 × PaCO2)). Enter PaCO2 and bicarbonate; the pH follows, and the five steps name the disorder and how far it is compensated.
calculators.formula: pH = 6.1 + log ( HCO3− ÷ (0.03 × PaCO2) )

steps.title: Step 1: pH
steps.text: Dissolved CO2 = 0.03 × {P} = {D} mmol/L; ratio = {H} ÷ {D} = {R}; pH = 6.1 + log {R} = 6.1 + {LG} = {PHR}. Below 7.35 is acidemia, above 7.45 alkalemia; within range, note which side of 7.40 it sits.

steps.title: Step 2: PaCO2
steps.text: {P} mm Hg. Above 45 pushes toward acid; below 35 pushes toward alkaline.

steps.title: Step 3: HCO3−
steps.text: {H} mmol/L. Below 22 pushes toward acid; above 26 pushes toward alkaline.

steps.title: Step 4: primary disorder
steps.text: Whichever number pushes the same way as the pH caused the disorder: PaCO2 means respiratory, HCO3− means metabolic.

steps.title: Step 5: compensation
steps.text: Other number normal and pH abnormal: uncompensated. Other number moved in the same direction as the primary one: partially compensated if pH is still abnormal, fully compensated if it is back in range. The two numbers moved in opposite directions: two disorders at once.

results.label: HCO3− : dissolved CO2
results.normal: About 20 to 1.

meaning.text: Normal acid–base values. pH {PHR}, PaCO2 {P} and HCO3− {H} are all in range.

Two primary disorders: respiratory acidosis and metabolic acidosis. PaCO2 has risen and bicarbonate has fallen, opposite directions, which compensation never does. Both lower the ratio, so the pH falls further than either would alone, as in cardiac arrest.

Two primary disorders: respiratory alkalosis and metabolic alkalosis. PaCO2 has fallen and bicarbonate has risen, opposite directions. Both raise the ratio, so the pH rises further than either would alone.

pH in range with only one number abnormal. PaCO2 {P} and HCO3− {H} give a pH of {PHR}, within 7.35 to 7.45. The stepwise method names a disorder only when the pH is abnormal or both numbers have moved, so it gives no label here. Recheck the values and interpret them with the patient.

Respiratory acidosis, uncompensated (acute). PaCO2 {P} is high from hypoventilation, and bicarbonate {H} is still normal, so the kidneys have not responded yet: typical of the first hours, as in an opioid overdose.
Respiratory acidosis, partially compensated (chronic). PaCO2 {P} is high, and over days the kidneys have raised bicarbonate to {H}, but the pH is still below 7.35: typical of severe COPD.
Respiratory acidosis, fully compensated. PaCO2 {P} is high and bicarbonate {H} has risen enough to bring the pH back into range, on the acid side of 7.40.
Respiratory alkalosis, uncompensated (acute). PaCO2 {P} is low from hyperventilation, and bicarbonate {H} is still in range, so the kidneys have not acted: typical of a panic attack, pain or fever.
Respiratory alkalosis, partially compensated. PaCO2 {P} is low and the kidneys have lowered bicarbonate to {H}, but pH is still above 7.45.
Respiratory alkalosis, fully compensated. PaCO2 {P} is low and bicarbonate {H} has fallen enough to bring the pH back into range, on the alkaline side of 7.40: as after weeks at high altitude.
Metabolic acidosis, uncompensated. Bicarbonate {H} is low and PaCO2 is still normal. The lungs usually respond within minutes, so this is seen only very early, or when breathing cannot increase.
Metabolic acidosis, partially compensated. Bicarbonate {H} is low, and deeper, faster breathing has lowered PaCO2 to {P}, but pH is still below 7.35: as in diabetic ketoacidosis or severe diarrhea.
Metabolic acidosis, fully compensated. Bicarbonate {H} is low and PaCO2 {P} has fallen enough to bring the pH back into range, on the acid side of 7.40.
Metabolic alkalosis, uncompensated. Bicarbonate {H} is high and PaCO2 is still normal.

Metabolic alkalosis, partially compensated. Bicarbonate {H} is high, and slower breathing has raised PaCO2 to {P}, but pH is still above 7.45: as after days of vomiting. PaCO2 rarely climbs above about 55, because slower breathing also lowers PaO2.
Metabolic alkalosis, fully compensated. Bicarbonate {H} is high and PaCO2 {P} has risen enough to bring the pH back into range, on the alkaline side of 7.40.

pH exactly 7.40 with abnormal numbers. PaCO2 {P} and bicarbonate {H} have moved together far enough to cancel out, so the side of 7.40 cannot tell you which came first. Consider two disorders at once.
No single number explains this pH. The values sit at the edges of their ranges. Recheck them, or consider two disorders pulling in opposite directions.
Next, calculate the anion gap to tell acid gained from bicarbonate lost, and check the compensation with Winter’s formula: expected PaCO2 about 1.5 × HCO3− + 8 (± 2).

calculators.exam: Nursing and paramedic exams label any gas with both numbers abnormal and a pH of 7.35 to 7.45 as “fully compensated”. In practice compensation rarely brings pH all the way back; the main exception is a respiratory alkalosis that has lasted days to weeks, and clinicians also consider two disorders at once. Use the exam label when a question asks for it.

presets.label: Worked example 6: three days of vomiting
Worked example 8: three weeks at altitude

asks.prompt: An ABG shows PaCO2 {P} mm Hg and HCO3− {H} mmol/L. Using pH = 6.1 + log(HCO3− ÷ (0.03 × PaCO2)), what is the pH? Then name the disorder before you check.

calculators.title: Anion gap
calculators.intro: In a metabolic acidosis, the anion gap tells acid gained from bicarbonate lost. Plasma carries as much negative charge as positive, but a routine panel measures only the main ions; the gap stands for the anions it does not measure, mostly albumin.
calculators.formula: Anion gap = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−)

steps.title: Add the measured anions
steps.text: {CL} + {H} = {MS} mmol/L.

steps.title: Subtract from sodium
steps.text: {NA} − {MS} = {AG} mmol/L.

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: With most modern analyzers the normal gap is about 8 to 12 mmol/L. Older textbooks give 8 to 16.

results.label: Anion gap
results.normal: About 8 to 12 mmol/L.

meaning.text: A gap of {AG} mmol/L is below the usual range. A truly low gap is uncommon. The most common cause is a low albumin, and a lab error is the next thing to rule out, so recheck the values before you interpret the bicarbonate.

High anion gap metabolic acidosis: acid gained. An acid’s H+ used up bicarbonate, and its anion, which the panel does not measure, took bicarbonate’s place. Think ketone bodies (DKA), lactic acid, kidney failure or poisons such as methanol or aspirin.

Metabolic acidosis with a gap that only looks normal. The gap is {AG}, but albumin, the largest unmeasured anion, is low; adjusted for it, the gap is about {AGC}. An added acid, such as lactic acid, is likely hiding behind the low albumin.

Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis: bicarbonate lost. Chloride, a measured anion, has replaced the lost bicarbonate ({CL} mmol/L), so the gap stays normal. Diarrhea is the classic cause; acetazolamide and some proximal tubule diseases do the same.
The gap of {AG} is high although bicarbonate ({H}) is not low. An added acid may be hidden by a second disorder that raises bicarbonate, such as vomiting.
A gap of {AG} mmol/L is normal: the unmeasured anions, mostly albumin, make up the difference.

Albumin is the largest unmeasured anion, and it is low here. The normal gap falls by about 2.5 mmol/L for each 1 g/dL drop in albumin, so a “normal” gap can hide an added acid. Adjusted for albumin, this gap is about {AGC} mmol/L.

asks.prompt: Sodium {NA}, chloride {CL}, bicarbonate {H} mmol/L. What is the anion gap?

calculators.title: Is the breathing keeping up? Winter’s formula
calculators.intro: In a metabolic acidosis the lungs compensate by lowering PaCO2. A rule of thumb from studies of patients predicts how far. A PaCO2 far outside the expected range means a second, respiratory disorder.
calculators.formula: Expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3− + 8, ± 2

steps.title: Allow ± 2
steps.text: Expected range {LO} to {HI} mm Hg.

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: Measured PaCO2: {P} mm Hg.

bands.label: measured is lower: extra respiratory alkalosis
measured is higher: extra respiratory acidosis

meaning.text: PaCO2 {P} is lower than the {LO} to {HI} expected. The person is breathing off more carbon dioxide than compensation explains: a respiratory alkalosis as well, as in aspirin poisoning, which stimulates the respiratory centers.
PaCO2 {P} fits the expected {LO} to {HI}: the lungs are compensating as expected for a bicarbonate of {H}, and there is no sign of a second disorder.
PaCO2 {P} is higher than the {LO} to {HI} expected. Breathing is not keeping up, so a respiratory acidosis is adding to the metabolic one: think of exhaustion, sedation or cardiac arrest.

asks.prompt: A patient with a metabolic acidosis has a bicarbonate of {H} mmol/L. Using Winter’s formula, what PaCO2 would you expect (the center of the range)?

calculators.title: Gametes from independent assortment
calculators.intro: In metaphase I each homologous pair lines up with the mother’s homolog facing one end or the other at random, independently of every other pair. Enter the diploid chromosome number to count the different gametes this alone can make, ignoring crossing over.
calculators.formula: n = 2n ÷ 2 pairs; different gametes = 2ⁿ; combinations when two gametes join = 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ

inputs.label: Diploid chromosome number
inputs.hint: A fruit fly has 2n = 8; a human has 2n = 46.

steps.title: Find the number of pairs
steps.text: 2n = {twoN}, so n = {twoN} ÷ 2 = {n} pairs of homologous chromosomes.

steps.title: Count the choices for each pair
steps.text: Each gamete gets either the mother’s homolog or the father’s: 2 choices per pair.

steps.title: Multiply the choices
steps.text: The pairs assort independently, so the choices multiply: 2 × 2 × … ({n} times) = 2^{n} = {gametes} different gametes.

steps.title: Two gametes join
steps.text: Any one of the father’s {gametes} kinds can join any one of the mother’s {gametes} kinds: {gametes} × {gametes} = {pairsOfGametes} combinations, before crossing over is counted.

results.label: Different gametes from independent assortment
results.normal: Human: 2²³ = 8,388,608, about 8.4 million.

meaning.text: A human can make about 8.4 million genetically different gametes from independent assortment alone. Crossing over makes the real number far larger, which is why brothers and sisters differ.

With {n} pairs, independent assortment alone gives {gametes} different gametes. Crossing over in prophase I multiplies that further, because it makes new chromosomes that are part mother’s, part father’s.

asks.prompt: A species has a diploid number of 2n = {twoN}. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can independent assortment make?

calculators.title: Counting cells through spermatogenesis
calculators.intro: Each primary spermatocyte completes meiosis I and meiosis II, and each spermatid then reshapes into a sperm without dividing. Enter a number of primary spermatocytes to follow the count and the chromosomes in each cell.
calculators.formula: Secondary spermatocytes = 2 × primary; spermatids = 2 × secondary; sperm = spermatids

steps.title: Primary spermatocytes
steps.text: {P} cells, each diploid: 46 chromosomes, 92 chromatids, because the DNA was copied before meiosis.

steps.title: After meiosis I
steps.text: Each makes 2 secondary spermatocytes: {P} × 2 = {S} cells, each haploid with 23 chromosomes still made of two chromatids (46 chromatids).

steps.title: After meiosis II
steps.text: Each secondary spermatocyte makes 2 spermatids: {S} × 2 = {T} cells, each with 23 single chromosomes.

steps.title: After spermiogenesis
steps.text: No division, only reshaping: {T} sperm, each with 23 chromosomes. Half, {X}, carry an X chromosome and half a Y.

results.label: Sperm made
results.normal: Four sperm per primary spermatocyte.

meaning.text: {P} primary spermatocytes give {S} secondary spermatocytes, {T} spermatids and {T} sperm. The same number of cells entering meiosis in the ovary would give only {P} oocytes, because each meiosis there casts off the other nuclei in tiny cells that break down.

asks.prompt: {P} primary spermatocytes complete meiosis normally, and every spermatid becomes a sperm. How many sperm result?

calculators.title: Ovulation day from cycle length
calculators.intro: The luteal phase is set by the corpus luteum’s lifespan and is steadier than the follicular phase, usually 12 to 14 days. So ovulation comes about two weeks before the next period, whatever the cycle length. Enter a cycle length (day 1 = first day of bleeding) and a luteal phase length.
calculators.formula: Ovulation day ≈ cycle length − luteal phase length (usually 14)

inputs.label: Cycle length
inputs.hint: Regular adult cycles run about 24 to 38 days.

inputs.label: Luteal phase length
inputs.hint: Usually 12 to 14 days; about 11 to 17 in real cycles.

invalid.text: The follicular phase would be under a week, too short for a follicle to grow to maturity.

steps.title: Use the steady phase
steps.text: The luteal phase, from ovulation to the next period, lasts about {lut} days.

steps.title: Count back from the next period
steps.text: Ovulation day ≈ {L} − {lut} = day {ov}.

steps.title: See which phase changed
steps.text: Here the follicular phase runs from day 1 to about day {ov}: {fol} days, compared with 14 in the 28-day model. The luteal phase is {lut} days. In most women, most of the difference in cycle length is in the follicular phase.

steps.title: Allow for real variation
steps.text: Real luteal phases run about 11 to 17 days, so in a {L}-day cycle ovulation could fall anywhere from about day {early} to day {late}. This is an estimate, not a date.

results.label: Estimated ovulation day
results.normal: Day 14 in the 28-day model cycle.

results.label: Cycle length

meaning.text: The textbook model cycle: ovulation on day 14, with 14 days on each side.

A {L}-day cycle with a luteal phase of {lut} days ovulates around day {ov}, not day 14. Its follicular phase is {fol} days, longer than the model’s 14, while the dominant follicle takes longer to be selected and to grow.
A {L}-day cycle with a luteal phase of {lut} days ovulates around day {ov}, not day 14. Its follicular phase is {fol} days, shorter than the model’s 14; the luteal phase lasts about {lut} days.

A {L}-day cycle with a luteal phase of {lut} days still ovulates around day {ov}. Its follicular phase matches the model’s 14 days, so here the whole difference from 28 days is in the luteal phase. That is the less common pattern: in most women, most of the difference is before ovulation.
Ovulation comes about {lut} days before the next period starts: around day {ov} of this cycle.
